Blaschke products associated to ellipses

Martin Baptiste, November 2026

A finite Blaschke product B of degree n sends the unit circle onto itself. Pick a point λ on the circle: the n solutions of B(z) = λ form a polygon inscribed in the circle. For some Blaschke products, all these polygons are tangent to one and the same ellipse. This page explains when that happens. The answer, Theorem Z, is my own result: a Blaschke product is associated to an ellipse if and only if it has one critical value in the disk, or two with simple critical points — a test that reads off \(B\) alone, in every degree, with an elementary proof. The surrounding theory (Theorems X and Y, the examples) is there to explain it. The page also contains a proof of a conjecture of Chiu and Ng on Shabat–Blaschke products.

The idea in three sentences

Take a Blaschke product B and a point λ on the circle. Its n preimages form a polygon, and the vertices of that polygon are the points you get by going back along B. Move λ around the circle and the polygon changes, but in some cases its sides all keep touching one fixed ellipse. The question is which B have this property, and how to recognise them from B alone.

Four theorems, in plain words

The paper proves three results about these Blaschke products. The first two describe them from the inside and organize classical material (the Poncelet package of Darboux, the elliptic curve of Poncelet's porism) around the Blaschke product. The third, Theorem Z, is the new result of the paper and my personal contribution: a characterization through critical values only, valid in every degree, which needs no ellipse at all. A fourth statement, Theorem L, was added in November 2026: it is not in the paper yet, it ties the first three to the theta functions of Chiu and Ng, and it is still being compared with the literature. A last statement, Theorem W, describes the curve touched by the polygons when it is not an ellipse, and has its own section further down.

Theorem X: the zeros are foci

Fix an ellipse \(\gamma\subset\mathbb D\) admitting circumscribed \(n\)-gons inscribed in the circle. The polygons come with a whole Poncelet package (Darboux): for \(k=1,\dots,\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor\), the diagonals \(z_jz_{j+k}\) of all the polygons envelope one and the same ellipse \(\gamma_k\) (with \(\gamma_1=\gamma\)), and when \(n\) is even the long diagonals \(z_jz_{j+n/2}\) all pass through one point \(P_{n/2}\) of the disk. Write \(\alpha_k,\beta_k\) for the foci of \(\gamma_k\).

Theorem X. Let \(B(z)=z\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac{z-a_j}{1-\bar a_jz}\) be a normalized Blaschke product of degree \(n\). The following are equivalent:

  1. \(B\) is associated to \(\gamma\);
  2. the zeros of \(B\) are \(0\), the foci \(\alpha_k,\beta_k\) of \(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\), and, if \(n\) is even, the point \(P_{n/2}\);
  3. \(B\) is, up to a unimodular constant, the product of \(z\), of the Blaschke factors \(q_k(z)/q_k^*(z)\) built from the dual conics of the \(\gamma_k\), and of \(\frac{z-P_{n/2}}{1-\bar P_{n/2}z}\) when \(n\) is even.

So the ellipse determines the Blaschke product completely, and conversely the zeros of \(B\) read off the whole Poncelet package. For \(n=3\) this is the theorem of Daepp, Gorkin and Mortini (the foci of the ellipse are the two non-zero zeros of \(B\)). The proof is a product computation: the two tangents to \(\gamma_k\) through a vertex \(z_0\) hit the circle at \(z_k\) and \(z_{-k}\), and \(z_kz_{-k}=\frac{(z_0-\alpha_k)(z_0-\beta_k)}{(1-\bar\alpha_kz_0)(1-\bar\beta_kz_0)}\) (Lemma 3 of the paper: the foci are the roots of \(F(\varphi,0)\), by Plücker's characterization of foci through isotropic tangents). Multiplying over \(k\) gives \(\prod_j z_j=B(z_0)\), so \(B\) is constant on each polygon.

Theorem Y: the hidden elliptic curve

A line through two points \(\varphi,\psi\) of the circle is tangent to \(\gamma\) exactly when \(F(\varphi,\psi)=0\), where \(F\) is a symmetric polynomial of bidegree \((2,2)\) computed from the dual conic of \(\gamma\) (Lemma 1 of the paper). Writing \(F=P(\varphi)\psi^2+Q(\varphi)\psi+R(\varphi)\), the discriminant \(\Delta=Q^2-4PR\) is a quartic whose four roots are the complex points of \(\Gamma\cap\gamma\): two in the disk, \(r\) and \(s\), and their mirrors \(1/\bar r\), \(1/\bar s\).

Theorem Y. If \(\Delta\) has four distinct roots, the curve \(C=\{F(\varphi,\psi)=0\}\) of pairs of endpoints of tangent chords is a compact Riemann surface of genus 1, isomorphic to the elliptic curve \(Y^2=\Delta(X)\) via \((\varphi,\psi)\mapsto\bigl(\varphi,\;2P(\varphi)\psi+Q(\varphi)\bigr)\).

The structure that comes with it (Lemma 5): write \(C=\mathbb C/\Lambda\). There is an even elliptic function \(f\) of degree 2, the inverse of \(\int d\varphi/\sqrt{\Delta}\), and a point \(\omega\) of the torus such that the point of \(C\) with parameter \(t\) is \(\bigl(f(t),f(t+\omega)\bigr)\). Going to the next vertex is the translation by \(\omega\): the vertices of the polygon through \(f(t)\) are \(f(t),f(t+\omega),\dots,f(t+(n-1)\omega)\), and the polygons close after \(n\) steps exactly when \(n\omega\in\Lambda\). This is Poncelet's porism, made linear. The translation itself is the composition of two half-turns of the torus — "other tangent through the same point" and "swap the two endpoints" — which is the whole content of Poncelet's theorem.

Combined with Theorem X, the Blaschke product becomes explicit on the torus:

\[ B\bigl(f(t)\bigr) = (-1)^{n+1}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} f(t+j\omega), \]

which solves \(B(z)=\lambda\) for every \(\lambda\) on the circle. When \(\Delta\) has a double root (\(r=s\)), \(C\) degenerates into two Möbius graphs, the vertices are the orbits of an elliptic automorphism of the disk, and \(\gamma\) is projectively a concentric circle: this is case (a) of Theorem Z.

Theorem Z: the test through critical values new result — Martin Baptiste, 2026

Theorem Z. Let B be a Blaschke product of degree n ≥ 3. Then B is associated to an ellipse if and only if one of the following holds:

  1. (a) B has exactly one critical value in the unit disk, or
  2. (b) B has exactly two critical values in the unit disk, and all its critical points there are simple.

Checking this needs only the critical points of B, which are the roots of a polynomial. No ellipse has to be computed.

An example from the literature. In Example 7 of B. Mirman, Numerical ranges and Poncelet curves, Linear Algebra Appl. 281 (1998), 59–85, the matrix with eigenvalues \(\pm1/\sqrt2\), each counted twice, gives a Poncelet curve of rank 5 which is not a conic. Theorem Z sees this at once: the corresponding product \(B(z)=z\bigl(\frac{z^2-1/2}{1-z^2/2}\bigr)^2\) has three critical values in the disk, \(0\) and \(\pm0.0566\), so it is associated to no ellipse.

The proof is elementary. Follow the vertices of one polygon while λ travels once around a critical value: the vertices come back, but permuted. The ellipse exists exactly when neighbouring vertices always come back as neighbours. In the two cases of the theorem, these permutations are exactly the symmetries of the polygon.

What is new, and what was known. Until now the ellipse question had been settled degree by degree: degree 3 always works (Daepp, Gorkin and Mortini, 2002), degree 4 works exactly for compositions of two degree-2 products (Fujimura 2013; Gorkin and Wagner 2017), degree 6 was treated by Hunziker, Martínez-Finkelshtein, Poe and Simanek, and Aksoy, Arici, Celorrio and Gorkin (2023) showed that a single critical value is sufficient and bounded the number of critical values in degree \(2^n\). Theorem Z replaces all of this by one condition on the critical values, valid in every degree. To my knowledge, the necessity of (a) or (b) and the sufficiency of (b) are new, as is the description of the monodromy group as cyclic or dihedral (Theorem Z′ of the paper), and the proof — a direct monodromy argument, which does not use the elliptic curve — is new as well. I would be glad to hear of any earlier occurrence.

Theorem L: the ellipses are Landen transformations observation, being compared with the literature

In case (b) of Theorem Z, the Blaschke product can be compared with the theta-function normal form of Chiu and Ng (see below). This links the two points \(r,s\) of Theorem Y to the two critical values of \(B\), through the classical modular functions. Write \(\rho(a,b)=\left|\frac{a-b}{1-\bar ab}\right|\) for the pseudo-hyperbolic distance, and \(k(\tau)=\vartheta_2(\tau)^2/\vartheta_3(\tau)^2\) for the elliptic modulus, with \(q=e^{2\pi i\tau}\). The explicit equations of the ellipses are given in the section From a Blaschke product to its ellipses.

Theorem L. Let \(B\) be a Blaschke product of degree \(n\ge3\) associated to an ellipse, with two critical values \(v_1,v_2\) in the disk, and let \(r,s\) be the roots of \(\Delta\) in the disk (Theorem Y). There is a unique \(\tau\) on the positive imaginary axis such that:

  1. \(\displaystyle \rho(r,s)=\frac{2\sqrt{k(\tau)}}{1+k(\tau)}\);
  2. \(\displaystyle \rho(v_1,v_2)=\frac{2\sqrt{k(n\tau)}}{1+k(n\tau)}\);
  3. the elliptic curve \(Y^2=\Delta(X)\) of Theorem Y is the torus \(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z)\), the Poncelet step \(\omega\) is \(1/n\) of its real period, and \(B\) is the Landen transformation of order \(n\): the isogeny of degree \(n\) onto the torus \(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+n\tau\mathbb Z)\);
  4. all the ellipses \(\gamma_k\) of the Poncelet package have the same points \(r\) and \(s\).

What is not new. Statement 4 is not new for circles: it is Proposition 4 of B. Mirman, Numerical ranges and Poncelet curves, Linear Algebra Appl. 281 (1998), 59–85. Mirman shows that when the curves of a package are circles, they belong to one pencil with the unit circle, with a common "imaginary chord" whose endpoints are the points \(r,s\). For ellipses, the statement still has to be compared with the pencils of Lomeli and Meiss (2023), whose invariant modulus plays the role of \(k(\tau)\).

In plain words: the distance between \(r\) and \(s\) gives \(k(\tau)\), the distance between the two critical values gives \(k(n\tau)\), and these two numbers are tied by the classical modular equation of degree \(n\). For \(n=3\) it is Legendre's equation \(\sqrt{k\ell}+\sqrt{k'\ell'}=1\), with \(\ell=k(3\tau)\), \(k'=\sqrt{1-k^2}\) and \(\ell'=\sqrt{1-\ell^2}\). So the points \(r,s\) determine where the critical values are, and conversely.

Idea of the proof. Up to automorphisms of the disk on both sides, \(B\) is the Chebyshev–Blaschke product \(f_{n,\tau}\) of Chiu and Ng, which satisfies \[ f_{n,\tau}\bigl(z(u)\bigr)=\sqrt{k(n\tau)}\,\mathrm{cd}\bigl(n\,\omega_1(n\tau)\,u,\,n\tau\bigr),\qquad z(u)=\sqrt{k(\tau)}\,\mathrm{cd}\bigl(\omega_1(\tau)\,u,\,\tau\bigr). \] The right-hand side is unchanged by \(u\mapsto u+2\pi/n\), so two consecutive vertices of a polygon are \(z(u)\) and \(z(u+2\pi/n)\). This parametrises the curve \(C\) of Theorem Y, and the first projection of \(C\) becomes the even elliptic function \(z(u)\). The roots of \(\Delta\) are the branch values of this projection, that is, the values of \(z\) at its critical points: \(\pm\sqrt{k(\tau)}\) and \(\pm1/\sqrt{k(\tau)}\). The same argument with \(z(u+2\pi j/n)\) gives the other ellipses of the package.

An explicit case. In degree 3 and in normal form, the ellipse has foci \(\pm\sigma\) and semi-axes \(\tfrac{1+\sigma^2}2\) and \(\tfrac{1-\sigma^2}2\), where \[ \sigma^2=\frac{3\,\vartheta_2(3\tau)\,\vartheta_3(3\tau)}{\vartheta_2(\tau)\,\vartheta_3(\tau)}. \] Every other Blaschke product of degree 3 with two critical values is obtained from this one by automorphisms of the disk: its triangles are the images of these triangles, and its ellipse is their envelope (it is not the image of the ellipse, since an automorphism of the disk does not send ellipses to ellipses).

Checked. For degrees 3 to 7 and Blaschke products in general position, with \(\Delta\) computed from an ellipse fitted on the polygons, statements 1 and 2 hold to 12 and 8 digits, and the \(j\)-invariant of \(Y^2=\Delta(X)\) equals \(j(\tau)\) to 12 digits. For the running example \(B_5\), the points \(r,s\) give \(\tau\approx0.5755\,i\); statement 2 then predicts \(\rho(v_1,v_2)=0.043525\), and the value computed from the zeros is \(0.043533\), the difference coming from the four-decimal rounding of the zeros. The proof above is a sketch; a detailed version will be added to the paper.

Symmetries: the dihedral group in action

Each time λ goes around a critical value, the vertices of the polygon are permuted. The permutations obtained this way form a group of symmetries of the polygon. Theorem Z says precisely which group occurs: the cyclic group when there is one critical value, and the full dihedral group Dn (rotations and reflections) when there are two.

LoopVertex j goes toType
around v₁4 − jreflection
around v₂−jreflection
once around the circlej + 1rotation

Two reflections one after the other give a rotation: going around v₁ and then around v₂ moves every vertex one step forward, exactly as one turn around the circle does. This is the content of Theorem Z in case (b): the group generated is the dihedral group D5 of order 10.

In case (a) there is a single critical value, the group is generated by one rotation, and it is the cyclic group.

The torus behind the picture

Theorem Y says that the whole configuration is governed by a torus \(E=\mathbb C/\Lambda\): an elliptic function \(f\) of degree 2 maps \(E\) onto the sphere, and \(B\circ f=g\circ\pi\) for an isogeny \(\pi\) and a degree-2 function \(g\). Below, the torus of the running example \(B_5\) is drawn as its fundamental rectangle — opposite edges are glued, as the arrows indicate — next to the disk it maps onto. Every object of the disk sits on the torus in the simplest possible way.

What the picture shows, reading the torus from its centre outwards:

The vertices are the coloured dots. They live on the two preimages of the circle, one dot of each colour on each (because \(f\) has degree 2, everything appears twice; the hollow dots are the second copies, running the other way). Press play: as \(\lambda\) goes once around the circle, each dot slides by exactly one step \(\omega\) — on the torus, going to the next vertex of the pentagon is the translation by \(\omega\). This is Poncelet's porism made linear.

The zeros of \(B\) are the gold stars: two horizontal necklaces of five, spaced by \(\omega\). They are the fibres of the isogeny \(\pi\) over the two zeros of \(g\): one necklace for the zero at the origin together with two of the \(a_k\), the mirror necklace for the rest. They sit close to the central line, but not on it.

The critical points of \(B\) are the crosses, at the half-steps \(\tfrac{k\omega}2\), \(k=1,\dots,4\), on the central line — the loop that \(f\) sends onto the hyperbolic axis of the ellipse. Odd and even \(k\) (the two colours) land on the two critical values of \(B\). The squares at \(0\) and at \(T/2\) are the points r and s, the roots of \(\Delta\) in the disk.

Checked. Everything in the figure is computed from \(B_5\): the lattice is rectangular to \(10^{-8}\), the vertex and critical rows sit at \(\pm h/4\) and \(0\) up to \(4\cdot10^{-4}\) (the noise of the conic fit), and the critical points sit at \(k\omega/2\) up to \(7\cdot10^{-5}\) — which also confirms, with exact values, the degree-5 claim of the working note of the next section. The two rows of zeros are at heights \(\pm0.030\): in particular the zeros of \(B\) are near the hyperbolic axis but not on it.

Where the critical points lie

Status. This is an observation from a working note, not yet a theorem of the paper. The sketch of proof is in the note; the step that identifies the real structure is still being written. What follows was checked numerically on the degree-8 example below.

In the degree-8 example, the seven critical points of B do not scatter in the disk. They all lie on one hyperbolic geodesic: an arc orthogonal to the circle (dashed), passing through two points r and s of the disk, which are the roots of the quartic Δ of Theorem Y that lie inside the disk.

What the observation says

  1. Alignment. The critical points lie on the geodesic through r and s, which is an axis of symmetry of the ellipse.
  2. Equal parts. Measured by the elliptic coordinate along the segment from r to s, the critical points cut it into n equal parts.
  3. Parity. The critical points with odd index lie above one critical value of B, those with even index above the other.
  4. Centre. The midpoint O of the segment is the hyperbolic centre of the ellipse. It is a critical point when n is even. The half-turn about O sends ck to cn−k.

What was checked

On the degree-8 example: the roots of Δ inside the disk are exactly r and s; the seven points are aligned on the geodesic through r and s; the midpoint of that segment is the critical point c4; the half-turn about it sends ck to c8−k; and the ratios t(ck)/t(s) equal k/8 to about 2·10−4.

The critical values and the canonical annulus

Where are the critical values of \(B\), and is there a geometric reason for the place of the zeros? Both questions have a clean answer, and the answer lives on a slit disk. Cut the disk along the hyperbolic segment \([r,s]\) of the previous section: what remains, \(A=\mathbb D\setminus[r,s]\), is a ring-shaped domain, and like every such domain it is conformally a flat cylinder. Its uniformizing coordinate turns out to be the elliptic coordinate \(u=\int dz/\sqrt{\Delta}\) itself.

Where the zeros are

The zeros of the normalized \(B\) form a regular \(n\)-gon of the annulus: they lie on the canonical circle through the origin, equally spaced for its angular coordinate. The critical points are the half-steps on the slit itself.

That canonical circle is an algebraic curve. Together with its mirror image under the inversion \(z\mapsto1/\bar z\), every canonical circle is a bicircular quartic; the one through the zeros passes through the origin, so its mirror passes through \(\infty\) and it drops to a circular cubic. For \(B_5\) (gold curve):

\[ (x^2+y^2+1)\,(0.57735\,x-y)\;-\;1.287351\,x^2+3.128323\,xy-3.114374\,y^2\;=\;0 , \]

which vanishes at the five zeros of \(B\). It is not a conic: the best conic of the pencil through the origin misses the zeros by about \(10^{-2}\).

Why the curve is algebraic

  1. On the torus, the canonical circle is \(f(L_c)\), the image of a horizontal line \(L_c=\{\operatorname{Im}t=c\}\).
  2. On that line, \(\bar t=t-2ic\).
  3. The real structure gives \(f(\bar t)=\rho\bigl(f(t)\bigr)\), with \(\rho\) the reflection in the circle of the axis; hence \(\overline{f(t)}=M^{-1}\bigl(f(t-2ic)\bigr)\) for a Möbius map \(M\).
  4. For any fixed shift \(a\), the pair \(\bigl(f(t),f(t+a)\bigr)\) satisfies a polynomial relation \(Q(x,y)=0\) of bidegree \((2,2)\): the addition theorem, exactly as for the Poncelet correspondence.
  5. So every point \(w\) of the curve satisfies \(Q\bigl(w,M(\bar w)\bigr)=0\): after clearing denominators, a polynomial of degree at most 2 in \(w\) and in \(\bar w\), i.e. a real curve of degree 4 whose top term is \((x^2+y^2)^2\) — a bicircular quartic. If the curve passes through \(0\), that top term vanishes and a circular cubic remains.

The same argument with vertical lines shows that the canonical radii are bicircular quartics too: the two families are the analogue, one degree up, of the confocal ellipses and hyperbolas given by \(\int dz/\sqrt{(z-a)(z-b)}\).

Checked. Canonical curves computed by a high-precision ODE (\(dz=P_1\sqrt{\Delta}\,ds\)) and fitted by a bicircular quartic: residuals \(3\cdot10^{-15}\) and \(8\cdot10^{-17}\) for two canonical circles, \(3\cdot10^{-14}\) for a radius; the same construction with the non-elliptic \(\Delta\cdot(1+0.3z)\) fails at \(3\cdot10^{-5}\). Repeated for \(n=5,6,7,8\): in every case the canonical circle of the zeros is a circular cubic (residuals \(10^{-14}\)–\(10^{-13}\)), all \(n\) zeros satisfy its equation to \(10^{-11}\), and a generic canonical circle is a bicircular quartic but not a cubic. The classical statement that these quartics are confocal, with foci the four roots of \(\Delta\), has not been checked here.

The critical values

Proposition. The critical values of \(B\) are values of \(B\) at the two roots of \(\Delta\) in the disk: \(v_{\text{even}}=B(r)\) for every \(n\), and \(v_{\text{odd}}=B(s)\) when \(n\) is odd (for \(n\) even, \(B(s)=B(r)\)). For odd degree, the two critical values come without computing a single critical point.

Theorem. With \(\tau\) the period ratio of \(dz/\sqrt\Delta\), and \(\lambda\) the modular lambda function, \[ \operatorname{cr}\bigl(v_1,\ 1/\bar v_1;\ v_2,\ 1/\bar v_2\bigr)=\lambda(n\tau),\qquad \tau=2i\,\operatorname{mod}\bigl(\mathbb D\setminus[r,s]\bigr). \]

Corollary. Up to automorphisms of the disk, the pair of critical values is a single real number, and that number is \(\lambda(n\tau)\in(0,1)\): the ellipse fixes the critical values of every associated \(B\) through the conformal modulus of one slit disk.

Why: the critical values of \(B\) are the four branch values of the degree-2 function \(g\) on the quotient torus \(E'\), whose modulus is \(n\tau\) because the isogeny divides one period by \(n\); and the cross-ratio of the branch values of a double cover of the sphere by a torus is the lambda function of its modulus.

Status. From a new working note (PDF). The proposition is proved. The theorem is proved at the level of the six-element orbit of the cross-ratio; which element occurs (the ordering of the four values) is fixed by the numerical checks above and remains to be pinned down by an orientation argument. The annulus statements rely on the torus picture of the axis note, whose real-structure step is still being written.

Degree 4: every possible case

In degree 4 the whole picture can be listed. First the parameters. A Blaschke product of degree 4 has four zeros and a unimodular constant; composing with an automorphism of the disk on the right moves one zero to \(0\), and composing with a rotation on the left removes the constant. What is left is \[ B(z)=z\prod_{j=1}^{3}\frac{z-a_j}{1-\bar a_j z},\qquad a_1,a_2,a_3\in\mathbb D, \] three free zeros, i.e. six real parameters; every degree-4 product is of this form up to automorphisms, and nothing below depends on the automorphisms. (One further rotation of the disk could fix the argument of \(a_1\), but it is more convenient to keep all three zeros free.)

Then the monodromy. Such a \(B\) has three critical points in the disk, counted with multiplicity. Going once around a critical value permutes the 4 roots of \(B(z)=\lambda\); the product of these permutations, in the order in which the critical values are met, is the 4-cycle given by one turn around the circle, and the indices of the permutations (number of points minus number of cycles) add up to 3. A 4-cycle factors in only four ways under these constraints, which gives four cases — and only four. Each case below is described by three things: its critical data (how many critical points and values, and which permutations), its parametrization (how to write down every \(B\) of the case, and how many of the six parameters it uses), and its geometry (what the quadrilaterals do).

In the figures, the sides of 72 quadrilaterals \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) are drawn in teal and their diagonals in orange: the envelope of the sides is an ellipse exactly in the first two cases, and the behaviour of the diagonals tells the cases apart at a glance.

Cyclic \(C_4\): one critical value

Critical data. One triple critical point \(z_0\); one critical value \(v\). The loop around \(v\) is the 4-cycle itself.

Parametrization. Every product of this case is \(z^4\) in disguise: \(B=\mu\bigl(e^{i\theta}h(z)^4\bigr)\) with \(h(z)=\frac{z-z_0}{1-\bar z_0z}\) the automorphism sending the triple critical point \(z_0\) to \(0\), and \(\mu(w)=\frac{w+v}{1+\bar v w}\) the automorphism sending \(0\) to the critical value \(v\). Up to automorphisms the case is therefore a single point, the orbit of \(z^4\). In the six-parameter family it is cut out by two complex equations, "the three critical points coincide"; in the normal form above (zero at \(0\)) this means that the three \(a_j\) are determined by \(z_0\) and \(v\): zero free zeros, two free points.

Geometry. Associated to an ellipse, case (a). For \(z^4\) itself (shown) the quadrilaterals are perfect squares, the sides envelope a concentric circle, and all diagonals pass through the centre; a general case-(a) product is the image of this picture by a projective map of the disk, and the circle becomes an ellipse.

Example shown: \(B(z)=z^4\).

Dihedral \(D_4\): the ellipse case

Critical data. Three simple critical points; two of them share one critical value (loop of type (2,2), a reflection), the third has its own (type (2,1,1), the other reflection).

Parametrization. Every product of this case is a composition \(B=C\circ D\) of two degree-2 Blaschke products, and conversely every such composition lands here (or degenerates to case \(C_4\)). Writing both factors in normal form, \(D(z)=z\frac{a-z}{1-\bar az}\) and \(C(w)=w\frac{s-w}{1-\bar sw}\), the case is parametrized by the pair \((a,s)\in\mathbb D^2\): four real parameters. The two missing parameters are the complex equation "two of the three critical values coincide" inside the six-parameter family: the zeros of \(C\circ D\) are \(0\), \(a\) and the two roots of \(D(z)=s\), so the \(a_j\) are not free but functions of \((a,s)\).

Geometry. Associated to an ellipse, case (b): the four roots sit like the corners of a square, the monodromy can only rotate or flip that square. The sides envelope the ellipse; the diagonals are the fibres of \(D\) and all pass through one point — the dark knot in the figure. In degree 4, "associated to an ellipse" is the same as "decomposable" (Fujimura; Gorkin–Wagner).

Example shown: \(C\circ D\) with \(a=0.5+0.3i\), \(s=-0.4+0.25i\) — the first two floors of the degree-8 example above.

Symmetric \(S_4\), degenerate: a double point

Critical data. One double critical point (loop of type (3,1), a 3-cycle) and one simple critical point (type (2,1,1), a transposition); two critical values. A 3-cycle and a transposition generate all of \(S_4\).

Parametrization. No closed form: the case is the hypersurface of the six-parameter family cut out by one complex equation on \((a_1,a_2,a_3)\), "two of the three critical points collide" (the discriminant of the critical-point polynomial \(B'\) vanishes), i.e. four real parameters. It is the wall between the generic region and the two ellipse cases: cross it and the two critical values of the collided points split again. Note the difference with \(D_4\): there two critical values coincide at distinct critical points; here two critical points coincide.

Geometry. Not associated to an ellipse: no ordering of the roots survives the monodromy. The sides envelope a convex oval which is not an ellipse (a piece of a sextic, the dual of a cubic), and the diagonals envelope a curve with cusps, which collapses toward the double critical point near the boundary.

Example shown: \(B(z)=z^3\,\frac{z-0.9}{1-0.9z}\).

Symmetric \(S_4\), generic

Critical data. Three simple critical points with three distinct critical values: three transpositions whose product is the 4-cycle. They generate \(S_4\).

Parametrization. The open dense case: any three zeros \((a_1,a_2,a_3)\in\mathbb D^3\) off the two walls above (critical values distinct, critical points distinct), all six real parameters free. "Generic" is meant literally — a random degree-4 Blaschke product lands here.

Geometry. Not associated to an ellipse. The sides envelope an oval (again a piece of the dual sextic), the diagonals a three-cusped curve. The alternating group \(A_4\) never occurs as the monodromy group: it contains no 4-cycle.

Example shown: zeros \(0,\ 0.5,\ -0.4+0.3i,\ 0.2-0.6i\).

The curve of pairs of roots

Two roots \(x\neq y\) of the same equation \(B(z)=w\) satisfy \(R(x,y)=\frac{B(x)-B(y)}{x-y}=0\). This defines a curve \(C\) of bidegree \((3,3)\). Forgetting the order of \(x\) and \(y\), and writing \(s=x+y\), \(p=xy\), gives a plane cubic \(E=\{F(s,p)=0\}\); the point \((s,p)\) encodes the chord joining \(x\) and \(y\), and the envelopes in the figures above are the duals of \(E\). Its shape tells the four cases apart.

CaseCurve \(C\) of ordered pairsGenus of \(C\)Curve \(E\) of unordered pairsHow to parametrize
\(C_4\), \(z^4\)three lines \(y=i^kx\)0, 0, 0a line and a coniclinear
\(D_4\), ellipsediagonals \(y=\sigma(x)\) and sides0 and 1a line and a conicrational, and \(\wp\) for the sides
\(S_4\), double pointirreducible, two nodes2smooth cubic, genus 1\(\wp\) plus a square root
\(S_4\), genericirreducible, smooth4smooth cubic, genus 1\(\wp\) plus a square root

In the \(D_4\) case the curve splits in two. The diagonals give a line in \(E\), whose dual is a point: this is why they are concurrent in the figure. The sides give a conic in \(E\), whose dual is the ellipse; on that component, moving to the next vertex of the quadrilateral is a translation of an elliptic curve, which is Poncelet's porism.

In the \(S_4\) cases nothing splits, but something elliptic survives: the curve \(E\) of pairs of roots has genus 1 even though \(C\) has genus 4 (or 2). One can then uniformize everything with the Weierstrass function \(\wp\): a point \(u\) of the torus gives \((s,p)\), hence a pair of roots \(\frac{s\pm\sqrt{s^2-4p}}{2}\), and the complementary pair is obtained by translating \(u\) by a point of order 2.

The genera can all be checked with the Riemann–Hurwitz formula. For instance, in the generic case \(C\to\mathbb P^1\), \((x,y)\mapsto B(x)\), has degree 12 and six critical values, each acting on the 12 ordered pairs with five transpositions, so \(2g-2=12\cdot(-2)+6\cdot5=6\) and \(g=4\). The same count on the Galois closure, where all four roots become single-valued, gives genus 1 for \(D_4\), 5 for the degenerate \(S_4\) case and 13 for the generic one: the curve \(E\) of pairs is the finest level that stays elliptic. This is special to degree 4, and comes from the exceptional homomorphism \(S_4\to S_3\).

Checked. The four monodromy groups were computed numerically on the four examples shown (orders 4, 8, 24, 24), the genera were recomputed with Riemann–Hurwitz, and the figures are drawn from the actual quadrilaterals \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) of these four products. The explicit uniformization of the \(S_4\) case is from a working note.

Degree 6: the eight monodromy groups

The same game can be played in degree 6, where the answer is richer. A degree-6 Blaschke product has five critical points in the disk, counted with multiplicity; the loops around its critical values are permutations of the six roots whose product is the 6-cycle of the circle and whose indices add up to 5. This time the possible factorizations were enumerated exhaustively by computer — every factorization of a fixed 6-cycle with total index 5, with the group each one generates. Exactly eight groups occur.

GroupOrderBlocks preservedLoop typesEllipse?Example
cyclic \(C_6\)6both(6)yes, case (a)\(z^6\)
dihedral \(D_6\)12both(2,2,2) and (2,2,1,1)yes, case (b)step-1 algorithm, \(n=6\)
\(C_3\wr C_2\)182 blocks of 3(2,2,2) and (3,1,1,1)no\(C(z^3)\)
\(C_2\wr C_3\)243 blocks of 2(3,3) and (2,1,1,1,1)no\(D(z)^3\)
\(C_2\wr S_3\)483 blocks of 2(4,1,1)+(2,2,1,1), or (2,2,1,1)²+(2,1⁴)no\(Q\circ D\) generic
\(S_3\wr S_2\)722 blocks of 3(4,2)+(2,1⁴), or (2,2,2)+(2,1⁴)²no\(C\circ P\) generic

Three things to notice. The two ellipse cases of Theorem Z fall out of the pure combinatorics: the only factorization by two involutions is (2,2,2)·(2,2,1,1), and it always generates \(D_6\). The block systems match the two ways of composing: a product \(Q\circ D\) with \(D\) of degree 2 groups the six roots into three pairs, the fibres of \(D\), joined by the long diagonals of the hexagons; a product \(C\circ P\) with \(P\) of degree 3 groups them into two alternating triangles, the fibres of \(P\). And one stratum splits: the data (4,1,1)+(2,2,1,1) carries two different geometries, the decomposable group of order 48 and the primitive \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\).

Cyclic \(C_6\): one critical value

Data. One critical point of multiplicity 5; one loop, the 6-cycle itself.

Parametrization. \(B=\mu\bigl(e^{i\theta}h(z)^6\bigr)\): the single \(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb D)\)-orbit of \(z^6\). Associated to an ellipse, case (a): here a concentric circle, and two more circles enveloped by the short and long diagonals, the latter all through the centre.

Example shown: \(z^6\).

Dihedral \(D_6\): the ellipse case

Data. Two critical values, five simple critical points split 3+2; the two loops are the reflections (2,2,2) and (2,2,1,1).

Parametrization. Case (b) of Theorem Z. In degree 6 this is the same as being a double composition \(B_3\circ B_2=C_2\circ C_3\) (the composition criterion of Hunziker, Martínez-Finkelshtein, Poe and Simanek), which is why \(D_6\) preserves both block systems. The figure shows the whole Poncelet package of Theorem X: the sides envelope the ellipse \(\gamma_1\), the short diagonals the ellipse \(\gamma_2\), and the three long diagonals meet at one point.

Example shown: output of the algorithm below for \(n=6\), centre \(0.1-0.12i\), ratio \(0.7\), inclination \(25^\circ\).

\(C_3\wr C_2\), order 18

Data. Two critical values, loops (3,1,1,1) and (2,2,2).

Parametrization. \(B=C\circ P\) with \(C\) of degree 2 and \(P\) a cubic with a single critical value (a disguised \(z^3\)); the smallest case is \(C(z^3)\). The two alternating triangles are the fibres of \(z^3\): the monodromy can only rotate each triangle and swap the two, never break them.

Example shown: \(C(z^3)\), \(C(w)=w\frac{s-w}{1-\bar sw}\), \(s=0.5-0.3i\).

\(C_2\wr C_3\), order 24

Data. Two critical values, loops (3,3) and (2,1,1,1,1).

Parametrization. \(B=T\circ D\) with \(D\) of degree 2 and \(T\) a cubic with a single critical value; the smallest case is \(D(z)^3\). The three long diagonals join the two points of each fibre of \(D\): the monodromy permutes the three pairs cyclically and can flip each pair.

Example shown: \(D(z)^3\), \(D(z)=z\frac{a-z}{1-\bar az}\), \(a=0.6+0.2i\).

\(C_2\wr S_3\), order 48

Data. Generic decomposable with inner degree 2: three critical values, e.g. (2,2,1,1)+(2,2,1,1)+(2,1⁴), or the special two-value data (4,1,1)+(2,2,1,1).

Parametrization. \(B=Q\circ D\) with \(Q\) of degree 3 and \(D\) of degree 2, both generic: the full symmetry of three flippable pairs. This is the decomposable side of the split stratum shared with \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\).

Example shown: \(Q\circ D\), zeros of \(Q\): \(0, 0.4-0.3i, -0.35+0.2i\); \(D\) as in the previous card with \(a=0.55+0.15i\).

\(S_3\wr S_2\), order 72

Data. Generic decomposable with inner degree 3: three critical values, e.g. (2,2,2)+(2,1⁴)+(2,1⁴), or the two-value data (4,2)+(2,1⁴).

Parametrization. \(B=C\circ P\) with \(C\) of degree 2 and \(P\) of degree 3, both generic: the two triangles can be scrambled independently and swapped.

Example shown: \(C\circ P\), zeros of \(P\): \(0, 0.45-0.25i, -0.3+0.4i\); \(C\) with \(s=-0.25-0.35i\).

\(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\), order 120: the exceptional case

Data. Two critical values: a triple critical point at \(0\) (loop (4,1,1)) and two simple critical points sharing one value (loop (2,2,1,1)) — the same data as a special order-48 composition, but arranged so that the group is primitive.

Parametrization. \[ B(z) = z^4\,\frac{(z-\tfrac12)(z-e)}{(1-\tfrac12 z)(1-\bar e z)},\qquad e=\frac{-87+416i}{850},\quad |e|=\tfrac12 . \] This \(B\) is indecomposable, yet far from generic: its group is \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\cong S_5\) acting on the six points of \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_5)\) — the exotic transitive copy of \(S_5\) inside \(S_6\), the one responsible for the outer automorphism of \(S_6\). Degree 6 is the only degree where a group strictly between the wreath products and the full symmetric group occurs.

Example shown: the boxed product.

Symmetric \(S_6\): generic

Data. Five simple critical points with five distinct values (five transpositions), and every remaining factorization type.

Parametrization. The open dense case: six random zeros land here. No block structure, no inscribed conic; the three envelopes are pieces of higher-degree dual curves.

Example shown: zeros \(0,\ 0.5,\ -0.4+0.3i,\ 0.2-0.6i,\ 0.1+0.45i,\ -0.55-0.2i\).

The Blaschke curve of the exceptional product

The curve of pairs of the degree-4 section can be written down for the boxed \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\) product too, and this time nothing is approximate: \(e\) has rational coordinates and \(|e|=\tfrac12\), so everything below is exact. Two roots \(x\neq y\) of \(B(z)=w\) satisfy \(R(x,y)=\frac{B(x)-B(y)}{x-y}=0\), of bidegree \((5,5)\); in the chord coordinates \(s=x+y\), \(p=xy\) this becomes the plane quintic

\[ \begin{aligned} F(s,p)=\;&6800\,s^5-(2704+3328i)\,s^4-(348-1664i)\,s^3\\ &-(2704-3328i)\,p s^4-24496\,p s^3+(7436+9152i)\,p s^2+(696-3328i)\,p s\\ &-(348+1664i)\,p^2 s^3+(7436-9152i)\,p^2 s^2+15417\,p^2 s-(2028+2496i)\,p^2\\ &+(696+3328i)\,p^3 s-(2028-2496i)\,p^3\;=\;0 . \end{aligned} \]

The point \((s,p)\) encodes the chord joining \(x\) and \(y\): it is the line \(w+p\bar w=s\). Three facts about \(F\), to be compared with the degree-4 table:

  • Irreducible. \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\) is transitive on the 15 pairs of points of \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_5)\), so the 15 chords of a hexagon — sides, short diagonals, long diagonals — all lie on one component. In the \(D_6\) case the same curve splits into a conic, a conic and a line (the two ellipses and the common point of the long diagonals).
  • Genus 2. The projection \((s,p)\mapsto w\) has degree 15 and four critical values: \(0\) and \(\infty\) (loop (4,1,1), which acts on the 15 pairs with index 10) and \(v_2\), \(1/\bar v_2\) (loop (2,2,1,1), index 6). Riemann–Hurwitz gives \(2g-2=-30+32\), so \(g=2\): the quintic has three singular points (one of them at \(s=p=0\), the triple critical point) with \(\delta=4\), and the Blaschke curve of pairs is hyperelliptic. In degree 4 it was elliptic; here one needs a genus-2 Jacobian to uniformize the pairs.
  • The envelope is a single curve of degree 12. The envelope of the chords is the dual of \(F\): the discriminant in \(p\) of \(F(w+p\bar w,\,p)\) factors as \(H(x,y)\,(x^2+y^2)^2\,Q(x,y)^2\), where \(Q\) is a conic with a single real point \((\tfrac{13}{46},\tfrac{8}{23})\) and \(H\) is an irreducible real curve of degree \(12=20-2\delta\), with integer coefficients and 91 terms. The three envelopes of the figure — the oval touched by the sides, the curve touched by the short diagonals and the small curve touched by the long diagonals — are three real pieces of this one curve \(H=0\).

Checked. The classification is an exhaustive computer enumeration of all factorizations of a 6-cycle with total index 5 (groups of orders 6, 12, 18, 24, 48, 72, 120, 720, and no others — in particular no group of order 36, 60 or 360). The eight products shown were then run through the numerical monodromy computation: each gives exactly its group, with the stated loop types. For the boxed product, the computed loops are (4,1,1) and (2,2,1,1) and the group has order 120. The quintic \(F\) and the degree-12 curve \(H\) were computed exactly (resultants over \(\mathbb Z[i]\), factorization over \(\mathbb Z\)); the contact points of the sides, short and long diagonals of the hexagons \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) satisfy \(H=0\) to \(10^{-50}\), and the genus and the degree \(12=20-8\) agree with the three singular points of \(F\) found by elimination.

The numerical range: the same curve, seen by a matrix

The curve touched by the polygons has a second life in linear algebra, and this is where the subject comes from. For a square matrix \(A\), the numerical range is the set of values of its quadratic form on the unit sphere, \[ W(A)=\bigl\{\langle Ax,x\rangle \;:\; \|x\|=1\bigr\}\subset\mathbb C . \] It is a compact convex set (Toeplitz–Hausdorff) which contains the eigenvalues of \(A\). For a \(2\times2\) matrix it is an elliptical disk whose foci are the two eigenvalues: the elliptical range theorem.

The matrix attached to a Blaschke product

Write the normalized product as \(B(z)=z\,\varphi(z)\), where \(\varphi\) has degree \(n-1\) and zeros \(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}\). The compressed shift \(S_\varphi\) is multiplication by \(z\) on the Hardy space \(H^2\), compressed to the \((n-1)\)-dimensional model space \(H^2\ominus\varphi H^2\). In a suitable orthonormal basis it is the upper triangular matrix

\[ A=(a_{ij}),\qquad a_{ii}=a_i,\qquad a_{ij}=\Bigl(\prod_{k=i+1}^{j-1}(-\bar a_k)\Bigr)\sqrt{1-|a_i|^2}\,\sqrt{1-|a_j|^2}\quad(i<j), \]

so its eigenvalues are the non-zero zeros of \(B\), and everything else is determined by them.

Theorem (Gau–Wu, Mirman; see Finding Ellipses). For every \(\lambda\) on the circle, the polygon with vertices \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) circumscribes \(W(S_\varphi)\): each of its sides is tangent to the boundary, and \[ W(S_\varphi)=\bigcap_{|\lambda|=1}\operatorname{conv}B^{-1}(\lambda). \] The \(n\) vertices are the eigenvalues of a unitary matrix of size \(n\) which has \(A\) as a corner.

So the Blaschke curve of \(B\) — the curve of this whole page — is the boundary of a numerical range, and “\(B\) is associated to an ellipse” means “\(W(S_\varphi)\) is an elliptical disk”.

The dictionary

Degree 3. \(A\) is \(2\times2\), so \(W(A)\) is an elliptical disk with foci \(a_1,a_2\): this is the theorem of Daepp, Gorkin and Mortini, and the reason why degree 3 always works.

Theorem Z, operator form. The numerical range of a compressed shift \(S_\varphi\) is an elliptical disk if and only if \(B=z\varphi\) has one critical value in the disk, or two with simple critical points. The test needs the roots of one polynomial, not the matrix.

The Kippenhahn curve. The boundary is only the outermost part of a larger object. Fix a direction \(\theta\): the hermitian matrix \(\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}A)\) has \(n-1\) real eigenvalues \(\mu_1(\theta)\ge\dots\ge\mu_{n-1}(\theta)\), giving \(n-1\) parallel lines \(\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}z)=\mu_k(\theta)\). The largest one is the supporting line of \(W(A)\). The envelope of all of them is the Kippenhahn curve of \(A\): a real algebraic curve of class \(n-1\) (dual to \(\det(x\operatorname{Re}A+y\operatorname{Im}A+tI)=0\)), whose convex hull is \(W(A)\) and whose real foci are the eigenvalues of \(A\). For a compressed shift it is the envelope of all the chords joining two points of a fibre of \(B\): sides and diagonals.

outermost and innermost branchesintermediate branchesmiddle branch (degree 6)eigenvalues = zeros of \(B\)
Checked. The theorem and Kippenhahn's results are classical; the figures are computed from the matrices, not from the polygons. For \(B_5\): the support function of \(W(A)\) equals that of the ellipse of the paper to \(10^{-15}\), and the two middle eigenvalue branches are tangent to the conic \(\gamma_2\) fitted on the diagonals to \(10^{-15}\). For the generic degree-4 example, the intersection of 4000 quadrilaterals has the support function of \(W(A)\) up to the grid error (\(2\cdot10^{-4}\)). For the \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\) product, the contact points of all five branches satisfy \(H=0\) to \(10^{-15}\).

Theorem W: the curve when it is not an ellipse

Theorem Z says when the polygons \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) are all tangent to one conic. When they are not, they are still all tangent to one algebraic curve: the boundary of the numerical range \(W(S_\varphi)\) of the previous section. Theorem W says how complicated that curve is. Its class, the number of its tangent lines through a generic point of the plane (2 for a conic), can be read off the monodromy group of \(B\) alone, by a simple count on the vertices of one polygon.

Chords and their lengths

Number the vertices of a polygon \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\) from \(0\) to \(n-1\) counterclockwise. The chord joining the vertices \(j\) and \(k\) has length \(d=\min(|j-k|,\,n-|j-k|)\), an integer between \(1\) and \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\): length 1 for the sides, 2 for the short diagonals, \(n/2\) for the long diagonals when \(n\) is even. There are \(n\) chords of each length, except for the \(n/2\) long diagonals.

The monodromy group \(G\) permutes the vertices, hence the chords. It contains the rotation \(j\mapsto j+1\) (one turn of \(\lambda\) around the circle), which keeps every length, so each orbit of \(G\) on the chords is made of whole length classes. Write \(D\) for the set of lengths that occur in the orbit of a side. Equivalently, draw the graph on the \(n\) vertices whose edges are the chords with length in \(D\): it is the smallest graph of this kind that contains the polygon and is preserved by \(G\). For a cyclic or dihedral group, \(D=\{1\}\) and the graph is the polygon itself; for the symmetric group, \(D\) contains every length and the graph is complete.

Theorem W: the class of the curve observation, proof being written

Theorem W. Let \(B\) be a Blaschke product of degree \(n\ge3\) with monodromy group \(G\).

  1. The irreducible components of the Kippenhahn curve of \(S_\varphi\) correspond to the orbits of \(G\) on the chords: the chords of one orbit all touch one irreducible curve, and the chords of two different orbits touch two different curves.
  2. If an orbit is made of the lengths in a set \(L\), its curve has class \(2|L|\), minus 1 if \(n/2\in L\).
  3. In particular the boundary of \(W(S_\varphi)\), the curve touched by the sides of the polygons, has class \[ m=2|D|-\mathbf 1_{\,n/2\in D}. \]

Theorem Z is the case \(m=2\): \(D=\{1\}\), that is, \(G\) preserves the polygon, that is, \(G\) is cyclic or dihedral. At the other extreme, when \(G\) can send any chord to any other, the Kippenhahn curve is irreducible, of the maximal class \(n-1\).

Why

  1. Chords move like pairs of roots. A chord of the polygon over \(\lambda\) is a pair \(\{x,y\}\) with \(B(x)=B(y)=\lambda\). When \(\lambda\) travels around the critical values, the pairs follow and come back permuted, exactly as \(G\) permutes them. So the curve of all such pairs (the curve \(E\) of the degree-4 section) has one irreducible component for each orbit of \(G\), and the curve touched by the chords of an orbit is the dual of that component. A line meets the circle in only two points, so different components give different curves.

  2. Counting the tangents from a point of the circle. The class is the number of tangents through a general point; take a point \(z_0\) of the unit circle. A line through \(z_0\) meets the circle at one other point \(y\), and it touches the curve of an orbit exactly when \(\{z_0,y\}\) is a chord of that orbit, for the polygon through \(z_0\). Now \(z_0\) is a vertex of that polygon: it has two partners at each length \(d<n/2\), one on each side, and a single one at length \(n/2\). This gives \(2|L|\), minus 1 for the long diagonals.

  3. The boundary. Every supporting line of \(W(S_\varphi)\) is a side of some polygon (previous section), so the boundary lies on the curve of the orbit of the sides.

A consistency check: added over all the orbits, the classes give \(2\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2\cdot\frac1n=n-1\), the class of the whole Kippenhahn curve of an \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) matrix.

For each length, the class is found as the smallest degree of a homogeneous polynomial in the line coordinates \((u:v:w)\) that vanishes on 1800 chords of that length (smallest singular value below \(10^{-9}\) relative to the largest). (*) For the long diagonals of the \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\) product the fit is ill-conditioned, because these lines almost pass through one point; the exact computation of the degree-6 section settles it, since a single irreducible quintic \(F\) contains all fifteen chords. The figures are drawn from the envelopes of the actual chords, not from the predicted curves.

What it says when \(B\) is not associated to an ellipse

Odd degree: the class is even. When \(n\) is odd there are no long diagonals, so \(m=2|D|\). Mirman's Poncelet curve of rank 5, which is not a conic, is therefore of class 4, the maximum: its Kippenhahn curve is irreducible.

Class 3 happens only in degrees 4 and 6. Class 3 means \(D=\{1,n/2\}\): \(G\) preserves the graph made of the polygon and its long diagonals, a Möbius ladder. For \(n\ge8\), the 4-cycles of this graph are exactly \(j,\ j+1,\ j+1+\tfrac n2,\ j+\tfrac n2\); a long diagonal lies on two of them and a side on only one. Every symmetry of the graph therefore preserves the sides, that is the polygon, and \(G\) is cyclic or dihedral: the ellipse case, with \(D=\{1\}\). The ladder only has extra symmetries in degree 4, where it is the complete graph \(K_4\), and in degree 6, where it is \(K_{3,3}\). So the boundary of \(W(S_\varphi)\) has class 3 exactly for the generic \(S_4\) case in degree 4, and for the products \(C\circ P\) with \(C\) of degree 2 and \(P\) of degree 3 (the groups of order 18 and 72 of the degree-6 table).

A quadratic outer factor. If \(B=C\circ P\) with \(C\) of degree 2 and \(P\) of degree \(k\), the two fibres of \(P\) are the sub-polygons of even and of odd vertices. A side joins an even vertex to an odd one, so it can only be sent to chords of odd length; in general position its orbit contains all of them, and the class of \(\partial W\) is \(k=\deg P\). The chords of even length are the chords of the fibres of \(P\), and they touch the Kippenhahn curve of \(P\) itself. For \(k=2\) this is the degree-4 ellipse case of Fujimura; the two figures above are \(k=3\) and \(k=4\).

Corollary (prime degree). Let \(n=p\) be prime. Either \(B\) is associated to an ellipse, and its Kippenhahn curve splits into \((p-1)/2\) conics (the Poncelet package of Theorem X), or its Kippenhahn curve is irreducible, of class \(p-1\). There is nothing in between.

Why: a transitive permutation group of prime degree is either contained in the affine group \(\mathrm{AGL}(1,p)\) or doubly transitive (Burnside). In the affine case, a translation is a \(p\)-cycle, of index \(p-1\); any other element \(x\mapsto ax+b\) fixes one point and has cycles of length \(o=\operatorname{ord}(a)\), so its index is \((p-1)(1-1/o)\ge(p-1)/2\). The indices of the critical values add up to \(p-1\), which leaves two possibilities: one critical value with a \(p\)-cycle (\(G\) cyclic), or two critical values with two involutions (\(G\) dihedral): the two cases of Theorem Z. Otherwise \(G\) is doubly transitive, so it is transitive on the chords: a single orbit, \(D\) is everything, and \(m=p-1\).

This is the geometric side of the statement “in prime degree, \(B\) is associated to an ellipse if and only if its monodromy group is solvable”. The monodromy groups of Blaschke products of degree \(n\) are those of polynomials of degree \(n\): both are given by permutations whose product is an \(n\)-cycle and whose indices add up to \(n-1\), and the Riemann existence theorem, applied on the disk, turns any such data into a Blaschke product. Müller's classification of the monodromy groups of polynomials (see also the section on dessins) then says which doubly transitive groups occur: \(A_p\) and \(S_p\), and the exceptional \(\mathrm{PSL}(3,2)\) in degree 7, \(\mathrm{PSL}(2,11)\) and \(M_{11}\) in degree 11, \(\mathrm{PSL}(3,3)\) in degree 13, \(M_{23}\) in degree 23 and \(\mathrm{PSL}(5,2)\) in degree 31.

Status. Points 1 and 3 of Theorem W are standard arguments, written out here for compressed shifts; point 2 is the count above. The automorphism groups of the Möbius ladders were also computed by brute force for \(n\le14\) (\(S_4\), \(S_3\wr S_2\), then \(D_n\)). Theorem W and its consequences still have to be compared with the literature on Poncelet curves and on Kippenhahn curves of compressed shifts (Gau–Wu, Mirman), where parts of it may already be known.

Dessins d'enfants: the tree of a Blaschke product

A polynomial with only two finite critical values (a Shabat polynomial) is encoded by a drawing: the preimage of the segment joining the two critical values is a tree in the plane, and the tree determines the monodromy. This is the simplest instance of Grothendieck's dessins d'enfants. A Blaschke product is never a Belyi function — its critical values come in mirror pairs \(v,\,1/\bar v\), so there are at least four of them unless \(B\) is \(z^n\) in disguise — but when it has exactly two critical values in the disk, the same drawing exists inside the disk, and Theorem Z becomes a statement about its shape.

Proposition (the tree). Let \(B\) have degree \(n\) and exactly two critical values \(v_1,v_2\) in the disk, and let \([v_1,v_2]\) be the hyperbolic segment joining them. Then \[ T_B=B^{-1}\bigl([v_1,v_2]\bigr) \] is a plane tree with \(n\) edges and \(n+1\) vertices. Its vertices are the points above \(v_1\) and above \(v_2\) (two colours, alternating along every edge), the valence of a vertex is the local degree of \(B\) there, and the permutations \(\sigma_{v_1},\sigma_{v_2}\) of the small loops are the rotations of the edges around the vertices of each colour.

Why: the segment has \(n\) preimages, the edges. If \(k_i\) critical points (with multiplicity) lie above \(v_i\), there are \(n-k_i\) points above \(v_i\), and \(k_1+k_2=n-1\) gives \(n+1\) vertices. The components of the complement of \(T_B\) in the disk correspond to the cycles of the loop surrounding both critical values; that loop is the circle, whose permutation is the \(n\)-cycle, so there is one component, an annulus. A connected graph with \(n\) edges and \(n+1\) vertices is a tree. The relation \(\sigma_{v_2}\sigma_{v_1}=r\) of the proof of Theorem Z says that the tree has a single face.

Theorem Z, read on the tree

“All critical points are simple” means “all valences are at most 2”, and a tree whose valences are at most 2 is a chain. So, among Blaschke products with two critical values in the disk:

\(B\) is associated to an ellipse if and only if its tree is a chain.

TreePolynomialBlaschke productMonodromy groupShadow of
star\(z^n\)case (a)cyclic \(C_n\)\(t\mapsto nt\) on a circle group
chainChebyshev \(T_n\)case (b)dihedral \(D_n\)an isogeny, modulo \(\pm1\)
anything elseother Shabat polynomialsnot associated to an ellipselarger—

The Blaschke products associated to an ellipse are the Chebyshev polynomials of the disk. \(T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos n\theta\) is the multiplication by \(n\) seen through \(x=\cos\theta\), exactly as \(B\circ f=g\circ\pi\) is an isogeny seen through the \(X\)-coordinate. (In case (a) there is a single critical value; the star appears when the second end of the segment is any non-critical point.)

The chain explains three facts met earlier on this page. Its two ends are the two vertices of valence 1, i.e. the non-critical points above \(v_1\) and \(v_2\): these are \(r\) and \(s\). They have the same colour exactly when the chain has an even number of edges, which is the distribution \((1,1)\) for \(n\) odd and \((2,0)\) for \(n\) even of the paper. The colours alternate along the chain: this is the parity rule of the section on critical points. And the chain is drawn on the hyperbolic axis of the ellipse, which is the alignment observed there.

Degree 4: all the trees

There are exactly three trees with four edges, and they are exactly the three degree-4 cases with at most two critical values. The generic \(S_4\) case has three critical values and no tree.

Star: cyclic \(C_4\)

\(z^4\), segment \([0,\tfrac12]\). Centre of valence 4 at the triple critical point; group of order 4.

Chain: dihedral \(D_4\), the ellipse case

\(C_1\circ D\), the degree-4 example of the paper. Three critical points of valence 2; both ends above the same value, as \(n\) is even. Group of order 8.

Fork: \(S_4\), double critical point

\(z^3\frac{z-0.9}{1-0.9z}\). One vertex of valence 3 (the double critical point), one of valence 2. Group of order 24: no ellipse.

Degree 6: one passport, two trees

In degree 6 the trees explain the split stratum of the classification. The data “one critical point of local degree 4, two simple critical points sharing the other value” — the passport \((4,1,1\mid 2,2,1,1)\) — is carried by two different plane trees. Around the vertex of valence 4, the two long arms are either opposite or adjacent. Opposite arms give a tree with a half-turn symmetry, and a decomposable product; adjacent arms give a tree with no symmetry at all, and the exceptional group.

Star: cyclic \(C_6\)

\(z^6\), segment \([0,\tfrac12]\). Group of order 6.

Chain: dihedral \(D_6\), the ellipse case

\(C\circ B_3\) with \(B_3\) of zeros \(0,\ 0.45+0.3i,\ -0.4-0.2i\) and \(s\approx0.0091-0.0185i\) given by the Corollary of the paper. Five critical points of valence 2. Group of order 12.

Opposite arms: \(C_2\wr S_3\), order 48

\(B(z)=z^4\,\frac{z^2-\frac12}{1-\frac12z^2}\), a function of \(z^2\): the half-turn \(z\mapsto-z\) is the symmetry of the tree. Decomposable, no ellipse.

Adjacent arms: \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\), order 120

The boxed exceptional product. Same valences as the previous tree, but no symmetry: the group is primitive.

Degree 11: a tree for the Mathieu group \(M_{11}\)

The Mathieu group \(M_{11}\), of order 7920, is one of the sporadic simple groups. It acts on 11 points and contains an 11-cycle, so it may occur as the monodromy group of a Blaschke product of degree 11 — and when it does, the shape of the dessin is forced. The non-trivial elements of \(M_{11}\) move at least eight of the eleven points, so their index is at least 4 (the involutions, of cycle type \(2^41^3\)), and the next smallest index is 6. The indices of the critical values in the disk must add up to \(n-1=10\), and the only way is \(4+6\). So a Blaschke product with group \(M_{11}\) has exactly two critical values in the disk, and its dessin is a plane tree. The passport is \((4,4,1,1,1\mid 2,2,2,2,1,1,1)\): two vertices of valence 4 above one critical value, four of valence 2 above the other.

The two trees look almost alike, and their groups differ by a factor of 2520. Moving one arm from one hub to the other is enough to destroy the structure of the Steiner system \(S(4,5,11)\) that \(M_{11}\) preserves. The tree is chiral: its mirror image, which is the dessin of the complex-conjugate product, has the same group \(M_{11}\).

The product drawn

The product is not rigid: for a fixed tree, the hyperbolic distance between the two critical values is a free real parameter, and the zeros move with it. They are therefore given numerically, for the parameter drawn above, in a normal form where one vertex of valence 4 is at \(a_0=0\) and another at the real point \(a_1\); the figure shows the same product composed with an automorphism of the disk. Each factor is \(b_a(z)=\frac{z-a}{1-\bar az}\).

\[ B_{M_{11}}(z)=z^4\,b_{a_1}(z)^4\,b_{a_2}(z)\,b_{a_3}(z)\,b_{a_4}(z), \qquad v\approx 3.4874\cdot10^{-5} + 1.2544\cdot10^{-5}\,i \]

How it was found, and checked. An enumeration inside \(M_{11}\) (generated by the 11-cycle and \((3,7,11,8)(4,10,5,6)\), order 7920 confirmed) lists the cycle types and their indices, which gives the \(4+6\) argument, and finds the pair of permutations of the tree. A numerical search for polynomials with this passport found six distinct trees; exactly one has group \(M_{11}\), the others generate \(A_{11}\). Each polynomial was then turned into a Blaschke product by shrinking it into the disk and following the solution as the critical values move apart. Along the whole deformation, the four simple critical points stay distinct, their critical values agree to \(10^{-13}\), and the group generated by the two rotation systems read off the computed tree is \(M_{11}\) (resp. \(A_{11}\)) at every step checked. The trees shown are normalized by an automorphism of the disk that puts the two hubs symmetrically about the centre, and the figures are zoomed on the trees (the unit circle lies outside the frame). The search did not find, in the time allowed, the tree of the other passport \((3,3,3,1,1\mid 2^41^3)\), which carries the group \(\mathrm{PSL}(2,11)\).

Degree 23: the tree of \(M_{23}\)

The same argument works for the larger Mathieu group \(M_{23}\), of order 10 200 960, acting on 23 points. Its involutions have index 8, the elements of type \(4^42^21^3\) have index 14, every other non-trivial element has index 12 or more, and the indices must add up to 22. The only way is \(8+14\): a Blaschke product with group \(M_{23}\) again has exactly two critical values in the disk, and its dessin is a plane tree with 23 edges — four vertices of valence 4, two of valence 2 and three leaves above one critical value, eight vertices of valence 2 and seven leaves above the other.

Unlike \(M_{11}\), this one could not be found by a blind numerical search: there are only four polynomial trees with group \(M_{23}\) up to affine maps, hidden among a great many trees with the same valences and group \(A_{23}\). They were computed by Noam Elkies (The complex polynomials \(P(x)\) with \(\mathrm{Gal}(P(x)-t)\cong M_{23}\), ANTS X, 2013), whose search for a first approximation took several days of computer time; his polynomials have coefficients in a quartic number field containing \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-23})\). The picture above starts from his formulas and turns the polynomial into a Blaschke product by the same deformation as for \(M_{11}\).

Elkies' polynomial \(P=P_2^2P_3P_4^4\) was rebuilt from the published coefficients for the four embeddings of his field: its eight simple critical values agree to \(10^{-13}\) (\(4\cdot10^{-9}\) for the second pair of embeddings). Along the deformation into the disk the eight critical values of the Blaschke product agree to \(10^{-12}\). At the parameters \(t=0.59\) (the one drawn) and \(t=0.73\), the two rotation systems read off the computed tree have the expected cycle types and generate a group of order 10 200 960. At some other parameters the numerical tracing of the 23 edges reads wrong cycle types; those readings were discarded, not counted as checks.

Where Galois theory enters

The monodromy group of a Blaschke product always contains the \(n\)-cycle of the circle, like the group of a polynomial (whose \(n\)-cycle is the loop at infinity). The primitive permutation groups containing an \(n\)-cycle are known, by a theorem of Feit and Jones resting on the classification of finite simple groups: apart from \(S_n\), \(A_n\) (\(n\) odd) and subgroups of the affine group of a prime field, they are the groups between \(\mathrm{PGL}_d(q)\) and \(\mathrm{P\Gamma L}_d(q)\) acting on the \(n=\frac{q^d-1}{q-1}\) points of a projective space, together with \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(11)\) and the Mathieu groups \(M_{11}\) and \(M_{23}\). For \(n=6=5+1\) the list reduces to \(S_6\) and \(\mathrm{PGL}(2,5)\): the two primitive groups of the degree-6 table, and nothing else was possible.

Blaschke products and polynomials have the same groups. Which groups of this list actually occur is a question about polynomials, already answered. The two problems have the same combinatorial data. For a polynomial of degree \(n\), the loops around the finite critical values give permutations whose product is an \(n\)-cycle (the loop at infinity) and whose indices add up to \(n-1\) (Riemann–Hurwitz). For a Blaschke product of degree \(n\), the loops around the critical values in the disk give permutations whose product is an \(n\)-cycle (the loop of the circle) and whose indices add up to \(n-1\). Conversely, such data, with any choice of critical values in the disk, is realized by a Blaschke product, by the Riemann existence theorem applied on the disk:

  1. The permutations define a branched covering \(S\to\mathbb D\) of degree \(n\), with the prescribed branching above the chosen points.

  2. Riemann–Hurwitz gives \(\chi(S)=n\cdot1-(n-1)=1\), and \(S\) has a single boundary circle because the loop of the boundary acts by an \(n\)-cycle. So \(S\) is a topological disk.

  3. Pull back the complex structure of \(\mathbb D\) to \(S\) and uniformize: \(S\) becomes the unit disk, and the covering becomes a proper holomorphic map \(\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\) of degree \(n\), that is, a Blaschke product.

So the monodromy groups of the Blaschke products of degree \(n\) are exactly those of the complex polynomials of degree \(n\), with the same branching data. The deformation used above for \(M_{11}\) and \(M_{23}\), from a polynomial to a Blaschke product, is one way of following this correspondence numerically.

The list. The primitive monodromy groups of polynomials were classified by P. Müller, Primitive monodromy groups of polynomials (in Recent developments in the inverse Galois problem, Contemp. Math. 186, 1995). Among the affine groups only the cyclic and dihedral groups occur (for prime degree, this is also the elementary argument of the corollary of Theorem W), and these are the two cases of Theorem Z. Apart from \(A_n\) and \(S_n\), the remaining groups are

and each of them is the monodromy group of a Blaschke product. On this page, \(\mathrm{PGL}_2(5)\), \(M_{11}\) and \(M_{23}\) are drawn with explicit products. In degree 8, trees with group \(\mathrm{PGL}_2(7)\) are drawn in F. Pakovich and A. Zvonkin, Minimum degree of the difference of two polynomials over \(\mathbb Q\), and weighted plane trees, where every other tree with the same passport has group \(S_8\); the deformation used for \(M_{11}\) turns them into Shabat–Blaschke products. The groups of degrees 7, 13 and 15 stand apart: according to M. Fried, Relating two genus 0 problems of John Thompson, they come in families with four branch points, that is three finite critical values. The corresponding Blaschke products, at least in these families, have three critical values in the disk, so they have no tree; their Blaschke curves are, by Theorem W, irreducible of class \(n-1\), since these groups are doubly transitive. What I do not know yet is which trees carry \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(11)\) in degree 11 (the passport \((3,3,3,1,1\mid 2^41^3)\) of the \(M_{11}\) section) and the groups of degrees 9 and 10, and how the curves of these exceptional products look.

When \(B\) has algebraic coefficients, as the exceptional product does, its monodromy group and its passport are the same for all its Galois conjugates: the group is an arithmetic invariant. What does not carry over from the theory of dessins is rigidity. A tree does not determine \(B\): the hyperbolic distance between \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) remains a free real parameter, which for the chain is the modulus \(\lambda(n\tau)\) of the section on critical values.

Status. The proposition is elementary and proved above; the reformulation of Theorem Z follows from it. Checked on the eight examples shown: the trees are computed by following the \(n\) roots of \(B(z)=w\) as \(w\) runs along the segment; each has \(n\) edges and \(n+1\) vertices with the stated valences, and the group generated by the two rotation systems read off the drawing has order 10 for \(B_5\), then 4, 8, 24 in degree 4 and 6, 12, 48, 120 in degree 6. For \(B_5\) the whole tree lies on the geodesic through \(r\) and \(s\) to \(3\cdot10^{-8}\), and its critical points to \(10^{-15}\). That the chain is the hyperbolic segment \([r,s]\) is, for now, a numerical fact: it should follow from the symmetry of the ellipse under the hyperbolic reflection in its axis, the same step that is still being written for the section on critical points. For the theory of dessins and trees, see Lando and Zvonkin, Graphs on Surfaces and Their Applications.

From an ellipse to its Blaschke product

Theorem X does more than describe the zeros of \(B\): it computes them. Here is the complete recipe, for any degree \(n\ge3\). It takes an ellipse and returns the associated Blaschke product; together with the test of Theorem Z, this answers the practical question entirely in both directions.

  1. Close the polygons. If the ellipse is only given by its shape (centre, ratio of the axes, inclination), first find the scale at which the Poncelet polygons close after \(n\) steps: the total angle turned in \(n\) steps of the Poncelet map decreases strictly with the scale, so one bisection finds the unique scale where it equals \(2\pi\). If the ellipse is already known to close, skip this step.

  2. Write the tangency equation. Let \(x^TAx=0\) be the equation of the ellipse \(\gamma\) and \(A^{-1}\) (in practice, the transpose of the cofactor matrix of \(A\)) the matrix of its dual: a line \(L\) is tangent to \(\gamma\) exactly when \(L^TA^{-1}L=0\). The chord of the circle joining the points with parameters \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) is the line \(d(\varphi,\psi)=\bigl(i(\varphi\psi+1),\ \varphi\psi-1,\ -i(\varphi+\psi)\bigr)\), so the tangency condition \(d^TA^{-1}d=0\) is a polynomial equation, quadratic in \(\psi\).

  3. Compute the quartic \(\Delta\). Take the discriminant \(\Delta(\varphi)\) of that quadratic. Its four roots \(\mu,\nu,1/\bar\mu,1/\bar\nu\) are the parameters of the four complex points of \(\Gamma\cap\gamma\): two in the disk, two outside.

  4. The elliptic coordinate. Set \[ F(z)=\int_0^z\frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{\Delta(\zeta)}},\qquad f=F^{-1}. \] \(f\) is an elliptic function; it can be written with a Jacobi function, \(f=\frac{\mu X-\nu}{X-1}\) with \(X(z)=\frac{1-\bar\mu\nu}{1-|\mu|^2}\, \mathrm{sn}^2\!\Bigl(z,\ \frac{|1-\bar\mu\nu|^2}{(1-|\mu|^2)(1-|\nu|^2)}\Bigr)\), or simply evaluated by numerical integration, which is what the figures of this page use.

  5. The step. Compute \[ \omega=\frac1n\oint_\Gamma\frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{\Delta(\zeta)}} . \] In the coordinate \(F\), going to the next vertex of a polygon is the translation by \(\omega\); the closure of step 1 says exactly that \(n\) steps make one period.

  6. The zeros, hence \(B\). The zeros of the normalized Blaschke product are \(0\) and the foci of all the ellipses of the Poncelet package (Theorem X), and these foci are \[ a=f(\pm j\,\omega),\qquad j=1,\dots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor \] (for \(n\) even, \(j=n/2\) gives a single point, the extra zero). Then \[ B(z)=z\prod_{k}\frac{z-a_k}{1-\bar a_kz}. \]

Worked out on \(B_5\), the running example: start from its ellipse (centre \(0.12-0.18i\), semi-axes \(0.9077\) and \(0.5446\), inclination \(30^\circ\)) and run the six steps. The roots of \(\Delta\) in the disk are \(\mu=0.7896+0.1524i\) and \(\nu=-0.4934-0.5692i\), one period of \(F\) around the circle gives \(\omega=0.9829-0.5675i\), and

\[ f(\pm\omega)=\{0.7488+0.1831i,\ -0.5088-0.5431i\},\qquad f(\pm2\omega)=\{0.6286+0.0042i,\ -0.1599-0.4510i\}: \]

exactly the four zeros \(a_1,\dots,a_4\) of \(B_5\) given in the first figure: the recipe recovers the product the figure was drawn from.

Checked. Theorem X is proven in the paper. The numerical pipeline above was run on \(B_5\): the elliptic positions \(F(a_k)\) of the four zeros equal \(\pm\omega\) and \(\pm2\omega\) (modulo the period lattice) to \(10^{-9}\), and the closure scale of step 1 matches the elliptic computation of the paper to all ten digits. The closed \(\mathrm{sn}^2\) form of \(f\) in step 4 is quoted from a working note and was not re-checked; the computations here evaluate \(f\) by integration.

From a Blaschke product to its ellipses: explicit formulas

The algorithm above goes from an ellipse to its Blaschke product. Theorem L allows the converse, with closed formulas: in case (b) of Theorem Z, the Blaschke product and all the ellipses of its Poncelet package are given by theta functions of a single parameter \(\tau\) on the positive imaginary axis.

The normal form

Put \(q=e^{2\pi i\tau}\) and use the single function \[ z(u)=\frac{\vartheta_2(u,\tau)}{\vartheta_3(u,\tau)},\qquad k=z(0)^2 . \] The Chebyshev–Blaschke product of Chiu and Ng is \[ f_{n,\tau}(z)=z^{\varepsilon}\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{z^2-b_i}{1-b_iz^2},\qquad b_i=z\!\left(\frac{(2i-1)\pi}{2n}\right)^{2}, \] with \(\varepsilon=1\) if \(n\) is odd and \(\varepsilon=0\) if \(n\) is even. Its critical values are \(\pm\sqrt{k(n\tau)}\), and the roots of \(\Delta\) in the disk are \(r,s=\pm\sqrt k\).

The ellipses

For \(j=1,\dots,\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor\), let \(\gamma_j\) be the ellipse enveloped by the chords \(z_iz_{i+j}\) of the Poncelet polygons of \(f_{n,\tau}\) (\(\gamma_1\) for the sides). It is centred at \(0\), with its axes along the coordinate axes: \[ \frac{x^2}{A_j^2}+\frac{y^2}{B_j^2}=1,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad |z-F_j|+|z+F_j|=2A_j, \] where

  • the foci are \(\pm F_j\), with \(\displaystyle F_j=\left|z\!\left(\frac\pi2-\frac{2j\pi}{n}\right)\right| =\left|\frac{\vartheta_1}{\vartheta_0}\!\left(\frac{2j\pi}{n},\tau\right)\right|\);
  • the semi-major axis is \(\displaystyle A_j=\frac{1+k}{\sqrt k}\cdot\frac{\zeta_j}{1+\zeta_j^{2}}\), with \(\displaystyle \zeta_j=z\!\left(\frac{j\pi}{n}\right)\);
  • the semi-minor axis is \(B_j=\sqrt{A_j^2-F_j^2}\).

How to read these formulas

The major axis is a ratio of hyperbolic distances. The point \(\zeta_j\) is a critical point of \(f_{n,\tau}\) on the real axis, and \(\pm\sqrt k\) are the points \(r,s\) of Theorem Y. With the pseudo-hyperbolic distance \(\rho(a,b)=\left|\frac{a-b}{1-\bar ab}\right|\), the formula reads \[ A_j=\frac{\rho(\zeta_j,-\zeta_j)}{\rho(r,s)} . \]

The foci. For \(n\) odd they are zeros of \(f_{n,\tau}\), in agreement with Theorem X (in a different order: \(\gamma_1\) is not the ellipse with foci \(\pm\sqrt{b_1}\) in general). They are the points \(z(u)\) such that \(z(u+2j\pi/n)=0\), which is the characterisation of foci used in Lemma 3 of the paper.

On the circle. The vertices of the polygons are the points \(z\bigl(t+\tfrac{\pi\tau}2\bigr)\), \(t\) real, and the polygon through \(z\bigl(t+\tfrac{\pi\tau}2\bigr)\) has vertices \(z\bigl(t+\tfrac{2m\pi}n+\tfrac{\pi\tau}2\bigr)\), \(m=0,\dots,n-1\). One also has \(A_j=\operatorname{Re}z\bigl(\tfrac{j\pi}n+\tfrac{\pi\tau}2\bigr)\).

An example

For \(n=5\) and \(\tau=0.35\,i\):

EllipseFoci \(\pm F_j\)\(A_j\)\(B_j\)
\(\gamma_1\) (sides of the pentagons)\(\pm0.937666\)\(0.991372\)\(0.321870\)
\(\gamma_2\) (pentagrams)\(\pm0.714008\)\(0.715488\)\(0.045986\)

In degree 3 everything collapses to one line: the ellipse has foci \(\pm\sigma\) and semi-axes \(\tfrac{1\pm\sigma^2}2\), with \(\sigma^2=3\,\vartheta_2(3\tau)\vartheta_3(3\tau)/\bigl(\vartheta_2(\tau)\vartheta_3(\tau)\bigr)\).

In general position

Every Blaschke product of case (b) is \(B=\varphi\circ f_{n,\tau}\circ\psi\) for automorphisms \(\varphi,\psi\) of the disk, and \(\tau\) is read on its ellipse through Theorem L: \(\rho(r,s)=2\sqrt{k(\tau)}/\bigl(1+k(\tau)\bigr)\). The polygons of \(B\) are the images under \(\psi^{-1}\) of those of \(f_{n,\tau}\), and its ellipse \(\gamma_j\) is the envelope of the chords joining \(\psi^{-1}\bigl(z(u)\bigr)\) and \(\psi^{-1}\bigl(z(u+2j\pi/n)\bigr)\). It is not the image of the ellipse above, since an automorphism of the disk does not send ellipses to ellipses.

Checked. For every degree from 3 to 8 and every ellipse of the package, with \(\tau=0.35\,i\), the chords of the Poncelet polygons are tangent to the ellipse given by these formulas to 12 digits.

A remark on invariant measures

The map that sends a vertex of a Poncelet polygon to the next one has invariant measures on the circle. In B. Mirman, Numerical ranges and Poncelet curves, Linear Algebra Appl. 281 (1998), 59–85 (Theorem 2), the measure is \(h(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta\) with \(h=1/\bigl((n+1)|\langle w,e(\theta)\rangle|^2\bigr)\). In the language of Blaschke products, the weights \(|w_j|^2\) are the Clark masses \(1/|B'(\zeta_j)|\) at the vertices, Mirman's Lemma 2 is the equation \(B(e^{i\varphi})=e^{i\gamma}\) rewritten, and \[ h(e^{i\theta})=\frac{|B'(e^{i\theta})|}{\deg B} . \] Mirman presents it as the measure of Kołodziej and King, which goes back to Jacobi. In the elliptic coordinate of Theorem Y, Jacobi's measure is \(dt\). The formulas above show that the two measures are different in case (b) of Theorem Z: on the circle, \(f_{n,\tau}=\Psi_{n\tau}\circ(\zeta\mapsto\zeta^n)\circ\Psi_\tau^{-1}\), where \(\Psi_\sigma\) sends the uniform angle \(s\) to the point \(z(s+\pi\sigma/2,\sigma)\), so Jacobi's measure comes from \(\Psi_\tau\) and Mirman's from \(\Psi_{n\tau}\). In degree 3 with \(\tau=0.35\,i\), the density of one with respect to the other varies between \(2.57\) and \(3.46\) instead of being constant. Both measures are invariant, since the polygons close, but they coincide only in case (a), with a single critical value, as for the concentric circles of Mirman's Example 3.

A proof of the Chiu–Ng conjecture

When a Blaschke product has exactly two critical values \(a\) and \(b\) in the disk, the preimage of the segment \([a,b]\) is a tree, as explained in the section on dessins d'enfants. Kenneth Chung Tak Chiu and Tuen Wai Ng call these products Shabat–Blaschke products, in their paper Hyperbolic Belyi maps and Shabat–Blaschke products (Journal of Mathematical Sciences, 2026). For a tree \(T\) with \(n\) edges and \(\tau\) on the positive imaginary axis, they consider the product \(B_\tau\) whose critical values are \(\pm c\), with \(c=\sqrt{k(n\tau)}=\vartheta_2(n\tau)/\vartheta_3(n\tau)\). When the tree is a chain, which by Theorem Z is exactly the case of the products associated to an ellipse, they compute the coefficients of \(B_\tau\) with theta functions. For the other trees they conjectured (Conjecture 11.1) that these coefficients are algebraic functions of theta quotients, and that they extend to the whole upper half-plane \(\mathbb H\).

Theorem

For every tree \(T\), the coefficients of \(B_\tau\), suitably normalised, extend to holomorphic functions on the whole upper half-plane \(\mathbb H\), and they are algebraic over \(\mathbb Q(c)\), with \(c=\sqrt{k(n\tau)}\). In particular the conjecture of Chiu and Ng is true.

The idea of the proof

On the Riemann sphere, \(B_\tau\) has four critical values: \(c\) and \(-c\) in the disk, and their mirror images \(1/c\) and \(-1/c\) outside. Written with \(1/c\) instead of \(1/\bar c\), these conditions no longer involve complex conjugation, so they still make sense when \(c\) is complex. For each \(c\), only finitely many normalised rational functions satisfy them, and as \(c\) moves they form the sheets of a finite étale covering of \(X_0=\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1,-1,i,-i\}\), the set of values of \(c\) for which the four critical values are distinct.

As functions of \(c\), the coefficients are therefore multivalued, like \(\sqrt z\) around \(0\): turning around one of the five forbidden values can exchange the sheets. But as functions of \(\tau\), through \(c(\tau)\), they are well defined, because no closed loop of \(\mathbb H\) gives a turn around a forbidden value. Indeed \(c(\tau)\) never takes these values, because the theta constants do not vanish and \(1-c^4=(\vartheta_0/\vartheta_3)^4\neq0\), and the half-plane has no holes. Turns around a forbidden value only come from paths of \(\mathbb H\) which are not closed, exactly as \(\log(e^z)=z\) is a single-valued function of \(z\) although \(\log w\) is multivalued.
