Poncelet from a pendulum

Everything on this page can be seen as mechanics. Take a point moving around the circle under a force that depends only on its position, \(\theta''=f(\theta)\), and look at it with a stroboscope: mark its positions \(z_j=e^{i\theta(t_0+jh)}\) at equal time intervals and join them in order. The sides of the polygon always touch one curve, and the closure does not depend on where you start: there is a Poncelet porism for every force. The question is which forces give which curves. Two harmonics give the ellipses of this page; the Blaschke products of this page are exactly the forces whose time density is a sum of Poisson kernels; and almost everything else gives curves that are not algebraic at all.

The stroboscope

Let \(f\) be smooth, \(2\pi\)-periodic and of mean zero, and let \(F\) be a primitive, so that the energy \(\tfrac12\theta'^2-F(\theta)=E\) is conserved. If \(E>-\min F\), the speed \(v(\theta)=\sqrt{2(E+F(\theta))}\) never vanishes: the point turns around the circle forever, with some period \(T\). Fix a time step \(h\).

Proposition (a porism for every force). (1) The polygon \(z_0,z_1,\dots\) closes after \(n\) steps if and only if \(nh\) is a multiple of \(T\); this does not depend on \(t_0\). (2) All the sides, for all the starting times, touch one closed curve; the side from \(z=e^{ix}\) to \(w=e^{iy}\) touches it at \[ P=\frac{v(y)\,z+v(x)\,w}{v(x)+v(y)}. \]

Why: the time \(\tau(\theta)=\int_0^\theta d\theta'/v\) is a coordinate on the circle in which the motion is uniform, so the time-\(h\) map \(x\mapsto y\) is a rotation by \(2\pi h/T\) in disguise. The side moves with \(x\), and \(dy/dx=v(y)/v(x)\); the envelope of a moving chord is the point that divides it in the ratio of the speeds of its two ends, which gives \(P\). The direction of the side, \(e^{i(x+y)/2}\), turns once, so the curve is closed; it is convex when its radius of curvature stays positive, which holds in every example below but not for every force.

Conversely, every curve with a Poncelet closure with the circle comes from some smooth force: the chord map \(g\) satisfies \(g^n=\mathrm{id}\), so \(g=\psi^{-1}\circ R\circ\psi\) for a rotation \(R\), and the speed \(v=c/\psi'\) and the force \(f=(v^2/2)'\) do the job. So the interesting question is not whether there is a porism, but which forces give which curves. The whole motion is encoded in the time density

\[ \rho(\theta)=\frac1{v(\theta)}=\frac{dt}{d\theta},\qquad t(\theta)=\int_0^\theta\rho,\qquad f=-\frac{\rho'}{\rho^3}, \]

and every positive \(\rho\) is the time density of a force.

Trigonometric polynomials: circles, ellipses, and then nothing algebraic

Let \(f(\theta)=\sum_{j\le N}a_j\cos j\theta+b_j\sin j\theta\). Writing \(z=e^{i\theta}\), the energy becomes \((z')^2=-2z^2\bigl(E+F\bigr)\): after clearing the powers of \(z\), the square of the speed of \(z\) is a polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(2N\), and the time is an integral \(t=\int dz/\sqrt{Q(z)}\).

  • One harmonic, the pendulum. For \(f=-\sin\theta\) the sides touch a circle: this is Jacobi's proof of Poncelet's theorem (1828). The motion is explicit: with \(\theta(0)=0\) and \(\theta'^2=2E+2\cos\theta\), \[ z(t)=\bigl(\operatorname{cn}(\omega t)+i\operatorname{sn}(\omega t)\bigr)^2,\qquad \omega=\sqrt{\tfrac{E+1}2},\quad m=\tfrac2{E+1}, \] and the period is \(T=2K(m)/\omega\).

  • Two harmonics, the ellipses. Now \(Q\) is a quartic and \(w^2=Q(z)\) is an elliptic curve: it is the curve \(Y^2=\Delta(X)\) of Theorem Y, and the physical time is the coordinate that uniformizes it. The stroboscope is a translation on this curve, which is Poncelet's porism in the form of Griffiths and Harris, and the sides touch a conic passing through the four roots of \(Q\), which are the points \(r,s,1/\bar r,1/\bar s\). Point 4 of Theorem L, all the ellipses of a package share \(r\) and \(s\), becomes obvious: they are one motion watched with the steps \(h=jT/n\).

  • Three harmonics or more. The curve \(y^2=Q(z)\) (or \(y^2=zQ(z)\) when \(N\) is odd) has genus \(N-1\) (or \(N\)), at least 2, and the stroboscope is no longer a translation on it. The sides still touch a convex curve, but generically it is not algebraic.

Three harmonics give transcendental curves proof sketched

Theorem. Let \(f\) be a trigonometric polynomial with \(N\ge3\) harmonics, and suppose that the Jacobian of \(y^2=Q(z)\) is simple (which is the generic case). Then for every step \(h\) that is not a multiple of \(T\), the curve touched by the sides is not algebraic.

Why: if it were, the correspondence \(z\mapsto w\) between the ends of a side would be algebraic and would lift to a curve \(\Gamma\subset X\times X\) on which the time form satisfies \(p_1^*\omega=p_2^*\omega\). The difference of the two Abel–Jacobi maps then sends \(\Gamma\) into the Jacobian \(J\), and \(\omega\) vanishes on the abelian subvariety it generates. If \(J\) is simple, that subvariety is \(0\) or \(J\); \(J\) is impossible since \(\omega\neq0\), and \(0\) would make the curve \(X\subset J\) invariant under a translation, impossible in genus at least 2 unless the translation is trivial, that is, \(h\equiv0\).

The exception that confirms the rule: if \(f(\theta)=g(k\theta)\) with \(g\) of at most two harmonics, the time integral comes from an elliptic curve, the polygons are fibres of \(B\circ z^k\), and the curve is the Kippenhahn curve of that product, algebraic. There is also no closed formula for \(\theta(t)\) when the genus is at least 2 (Briot–Bouquet), but the solution is still explicit as a Fourier series: \(e^{i\theta(t)}=\sum_k c_k e^{2\pi ikt/T}\), with \(c_k=\frac1T\int_0^{2\pi}e^{\,i\theta-2\pi ik\,t(\theta)/T}\rho(\theta)\,d\theta\).

Checked. For each force, 80 sides are computed with 40 digits, and we look for a polynomial \(P(z,w)\) of bidegree \((d,d)\) vanishing at the two ends of every side. The table gives the smallest singular value of the system (relative): an algebraic relation shows up as a sudden drop to the working precision.

Force \(f\)\(d=2\)\(d=4\)\(d=6\)\(d=7\)
\(-\sin\theta-0.3\sin2\theta\)\(3\cdot10^{-41}\)
\(-\sin3\theta\) (\(=g(3\theta)\))\(5\cdot10^{-5}\)\(3\cdot10^{-15}\)\(2\cdot10^{-41}\)
\(-\sin\theta+0.2\cos3\theta\)\(4\cdot10^{-5}\)\(3\cdot10^{-12}\)\(4\cdot10^{-23}\)\(2\cdot10^{-29}\)

The two harmonics drop at the bidegree of Poncelet's correspondence, \((2,2)\); the force \(g(3\theta)\) at \((6,6)\), as predicted; the generic three-harmonic force decreases steadily, with no drop.

Rational forces: the Blaschke products come back

Allow now \(f\) to be a rational function of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\). The key is a classical identity: for a Blaschke product \(B\) with zeros \(a_j\),

\[ |B'(e^{i\theta})|=\sum_j P_{a_j}(\theta),\qquad P_a(\theta)=\frac{1-|a|^2}{|e^{i\theta}-a|^2}\quad\text{(the Poisson kernel).} \]

So take the time density \(\rho=\sum_jP_{a_j}\). Then \(t(\theta)=\arg B(e^{i\theta})\): the value of \(B\) turns around the circle at constant speed, and the stroboscope with step \(h=2\pi\) draws exactly the fibres \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\). The force is \(f=-\rho'/\rho^3\), rational in \(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\); it is smooth on the circle, and its singularities, for complex \(\theta\), sit at the critical points of \(B\), where \(\rho\) vanishes. The motion is explicit and algebraic: \(z(t)\) is a root of \(B(z)=e^{it}\). Every Blaschke product of this page is a rational force. Among the trigonometric polynomials, only the powers \(\varphi_a^n\) of a disk automorphism were: for them the speed \[ v=\frac1\rho=\frac{|e^{i\theta}-a|^2}{n(1-|a|^2)} \] is a trigonometric polynomial, the force has two harmonics, and the curve is an ellipse (checked: a conic to \(5\cdot10^{-15}\), not a circle).

The equation of a Blaschke product, concretely. Write the zeros as \(a_j=r_je^{i\alpha_j}\) and \(D_j(\theta)=1+r_j^2-2r_j\cos(\theta-\alpha_j)\). The motion of \(B\) is

\[ \theta''=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_j\frac{2r_j(1-r_j^2)\sin(\theta-\alpha_j)}{D_j(\theta)^2}} {\Bigl(\displaystyle\sum_j\frac{1-r_j^2}{D_j(\theta)}\Bigr)^{3}}, \qquad \theta'(0)=\frac1{|B'(e^{i\theta(0)})|}, \]

and the initial speed matters: the same force at any other energy gives another motion, whose polygons are not fibres of \(B\). The first-order form is simpler still, and holomorphic:

\[ z'=i\,\frac{B(z)}{B'(z)},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad \bigl(B(z)\bigr)'=iB(z),\quad B(z(t))=B(z(0))\,e^{it}. \]

Example. For \(B(z)=z^2\,\dfrac{z-\frac12}{1-\frac z2}\), the time density is \(\rho=2+\dfrac{3}{5-4\cos\theta}\), and the equation is

\[ \theta''=\frac{12\sin\theta\,(5-4\cos\theta)}{(13-8\cos\theta)^3},\qquad \theta(0)=0,\quad\theta'(0)=\tfrac15. \]

The period is \(6\pi\); the stroboscope with step \(2\pi\) draws triangles, the fibres of \(B\), all tangent to the ellipse with foci \(0\) and \(\tfrac12\) (Theorem X). Checked: \(B\) takes the same value at the three vertices, and \(B(z(t))=e^{it}\), to the integration accuracy; with \(\theta'(0)=0.3\) instead, the three values differ.

Kepler's equation. The time density \(\rho=1+\varepsilon\cos\theta\) is the simplest one that is not a Blaschke clock. It gives the force and the time

\[ \theta''=\frac{\varepsilon\sin\theta}{(1+\varepsilon\cos\theta)^3},\qquad t=\theta+\varepsilon\sin\theta, \]

and the second equation is Kepler's equation: with \(\theta(0)=\pi\), the angle \(\theta-\pi\) is the eccentric anomaly of a planet on an orbit of eccentricity \(\varepsilon\). The stroboscopic polygons are the positions, at equal times, of the point of the planet on the auxiliary circle of its orbit. The solution is explicit, by Bessel's series:

\[ \theta(t)=\pi+t+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac2k\,J_k(k\varepsilon)\sin(kt), \]

checked against a numerical integration to \(6\cdot10^{-12}\). It is the Fourier formula above in this case.

Which rational time densities give algebraic curves proof sketched

Theorem. Let \(\rho\) be a positive rational function of \(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\), and \(h\) a step that is not a multiple of \(T\). The sides touch an algebraic curve if and only if \[ \rho\,d\theta=\frac1{ic}\,d\log\frac{B_1}{B_2} \] for two finite Blaschke products \(B_1,B_2\); equivalently, \(\rho=\sum_k w_kP_{a_k}\) with real weights \(w_k\) (of any sign) that are all rational multiples of one number. The polygons are then pieces of the fibres of a power of \(B_1/B_2\), and the curves are Kippenhahn curves.

Why: \(dt=\rho\,d\theta\) is a rational differential on the Riemann sphere. Each simple pole \(a_k\) inside the disk contributes \(w_k\arg\varphi_{a_k}\) to the time; a complex residue adds a term in \(\log|e^{i\theta}-a_k|\), and a pole of higher order a rational term. The relation between the ends of a side reads \[ \sum_kw_k\bigl[\log\varphi_{a_k}(w)-\log\varphi_{a_k}(z)\bigr]+R(w)-R(z)=ih. \] If it were algebraic, the logarithms \(\log\bigl(\varphi_{a_k}(w)/\varphi_{a_k}(z)\bigr)\) would be logarithms of algebraic functions on a curve, and Ax's theorem (the functional Schanuel conjecture, 1971) makes them algebraically independent, except for \(\mathbb Q\)-linear relations. This forces \(R\) constant, the residues purely imaginary, and the weights commensurable. In words: two clocks running at incommensurable rates cannot be tied by an algebraic relation.

Checked. The same test as above, with 125 sides computed with 90 digits, for \(a=0.3+0.2i\), \(b=-0.4+0.35i\) and a step \(h=1.1\) that does not close the polygons:

Time density \(\rho\)\(d=3\)\(d=5\)\(d=7\)\(d=9\)
\(P_a+2P_b\) (\(B=\varphi_a\varphi_b^2\))\(7\cdot10^{-91}\)
\(P_a+\sqrt2\,P_b\)\(10^{-11}\)\(4\cdot10^{-28}\)\(3\cdot10^{-53}\)\(3\cdot10^{-86}\)
\(1+0.3\cos\theta\) (Kepler)\(2\cdot10^{-11}\)\(6\cdot10^{-28}\)\(10^{-52}\)\(6\cdot10^{-86}\)

The Blaschke clock drops to the working precision at once, at the degree of \(B\). The other two decrease faster and faster but never drop: the gaps between consecutive degrees grow (8, 9, 11, 14, 16, 17 orders of magnitude), which is what one expects when polynomials approximate a relation of exponential type.

Two clocks. This gives a new reading of Theorem Z. The polygons of a Poncelet package around an ellipse are produced by two different forces: a two-harmonic force, whose clock is an elliptic curve, and the Blaschke clock \(\rho=|B'|\), whose clock is the multiplicative group. A Blaschke product that is not associated to an ellipse has only the second clock.

Conjecture. For a general rational force, the time is an abelian integral of the third kind, and the stroboscope is a translation in a generalized Jacobian, an extension of an abelian variety by a torus. The curve should be algebraic exactly when the time comes from an algebraic group of dimension 1: the multiplicative group (a Blaschke clock) or an elliptic curve (a Poncelet conic). The additive group is excluded, since a rational function cannot grow by \(T\) at each turn. Ax also proved his theorem for these semi-abelian varieties (1972).

Fractional harmonics: star polygons

Allow finally \(\cos(j\theta/k)\) and \(\sin(j\theta/k)\) in \(f\). The force now has period \(2\pi k\), so the position \(z=e^{i\theta}\) no longer determines the speed. Write \(\varphi=\theta/k\) and \(u=e^{i\varphi}\): the angle \(\varphi\) obeys \(\varphi''=f(k\varphi)/k\), an equation of the previous kind, and \(z=u^k\). The stroboscope on \(z\) is the shadow, under \(u\mapsto u^k\), of a stroboscope on \(u\). Everything follows from this:

  1. Star polygons. With \(h=T/n\), where \(T\) is the period of \(\varphi\), the \(n\) vertices wind \(k\) times around the circle. Through each point pass \(k\) polygons, one for each \(k\)-th root \(u\).

  2. A curve that turns \(k\) times. The direction of a side, \(e^{ik(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)/2}\), turns \(k\) times when \(u\) goes around once. From a point of the circle, \(k\) lifts and two sides each give \(2k\) tangents: the class is \(2k\). Checked: rotation index 2.0000 and class 4 for \(k=2\); 3.0000 and class 6 for \(k=3\).

  3. Algebraic in the same cases. Count the harmonics in units of \(\theta/k\): at most two (or a Blaschke clock in \(u\)), the curve is algebraic; otherwise it is not.

  4. A porism, with extra closed polygons. When \(nh\) is a multiple of the period \(T\) of \(\varphi\), every polygon closes after \(n\) steps: the porism holds. But the polygon on \(z\) also closes as soon as \(\varphi\) advances by a multiple of \(2\pi/k\), and that advance depends on the starting point. So, for other steps, isolated closed polygons appear whose neighbours do not close: the rule that one closed polygon forces all the others to close fails for them.

The half-pendulum, explicitly. With \(\theta(0)=0\) and \(\theta'(0)=2\sqrt3\), the angle \(\varphi=\theta/2\) is an ordinary pendulum, and

\[ z(t)=\bigl(\operatorname{cn}(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2t)+i\operatorname{sn}(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2t)\bigr)^4,\qquad m=\tfrac23, \]

with period \(T=4K(2/3)/\sqrt3\approx4.6857\) (checked to \(3\cdot10^{-12}\)).

An isolated closed triangle. The pentagrams of the figure all close (\(5h=T\)): that is the porism. Now take three steps of \(T/6\). Depending on the starting point, \(\theta\) advances by between \(5.198\) and \(7.368\) after three steps: the triangle closes only when this is \(2\pi\), which happens for exactly two starting angles, \(\varphi_0=0\) and \(\pi\), that is, for a single closed triangle through \(z=1\). This triangle is inscribed in the circle and circumscribed about the curve of step \(T/6\), yet its neighbours do not close. With three steps of \(T/3\), \(\theta\) advances by \(4\pi\) from every start, and every triangle closes.

The first two have one and two harmonics in units of \(\theta/2\) and drop at bidegree \((4,4)\): each end has two lifts, each with two neighbours. The third has three and does not drop.

Status. The porism for every force, the contact point, the circle (one harmonic), the conic (two harmonics), the Blaschke clocks, Kepler's case and the reduction of fractional harmonics are proved above, and all the formulas were checked numerically. The two transcendence theorems are sketched: the first needs the genericity of a simple Jacobian to be made precise for this real family, the second a careful application of Ax's theorem. The semi-abelian statement is a conjecture. The tables are numerical evidence, not proofs.

Note: Blaschke clocks, harmonics, and the trees they count

The previous section showed that every Blaschke product is a mechanical system: a point moving on the circle under a force \(\theta''=f(\theta)\), photographed at equal time intervals, draws the polygons \(B^{-1}(\lambda)\). This note follows that idea further. It asks three questions. Which forces draw the polygons of a given \(B\)? How simple can such a force be? And what do we end up counting when we sort the answers? The last question leads to integer sequences, some already in the OEIS and some apparently not.

1. Every motion that draws the polygons of \(B\)

The force of the Blaschke clock makes the value of \(B\) turn at constant speed. It is not the only force that works. A motion draws the polygons of \(B\) as soon as the time it needs to go from one vertex to the next is always the same. So we may speed the clock up or slow it down, as long as the change depends only on the value of \(B\), which is the same at all the vertices of a polygon.

Proposition. A rotating motion draws the polygons of \(B\) if and only if the square of its speed has the form \[ v(\theta)^2=\frac{\Phi\bigl(B(e^{i\theta})\bigr)}{|B'(e^{i\theta})|^2}, \] where \(\Phi\) is any positive function on the circle. The force is then \(f=(v^2/2)'\).

Why: in the coordinate \(s=\arg B(e^{i\theta})\), the next vertex is always \(s+2\pi\). The time spent between two vertices is constant exactly when the time, written as a function of \(s\), is a linear function plus a \(2\pi\)-periodic one. Differentiating gives the formula, with \(1/\sqrt\Phi\) the derivative of the periodic part.

2. When is the force a trigonometric polynomial?

A force with finitely many harmonics, like the pendulum, is the simplest kind. Here is exactly when \(B\) has one. Compose \(B\) on the left with a disk automorphism so that \(B(0)=0\); this changes neither the polygons nor the question. Then read three numbers off \(B\):

  • \(m\): the order of the zero of \(B\) at the centre of the disk (\(m=1\) when the centre is not a critical point);
  • \(M\): the largest multiplicity among the other zeros of \(B\);
  • \(W\): the weight of the critical values of \(B\) other than \(0\). Each of them counts \(1\) if all its critical points are simple, and \(2\) otherwise.

The harmonic criterion proof outlined

Theorem. Let \(B\neq z^n\) with \(B(0)=0\). Its polygons are drawn by a force with finitely many harmonics if and only if \(W\cdot M\le2\). The smallest possible number of harmonics is then exactly \(m\cdot W\), reached with \(\Phi(w)=\prod_v|w-v|^2\) over the critical values \(v\neq0\) (a factor squared when its weight is 2).

  1. \(\Phi\) is rational. If the force is a trigonometric polynomial, \(v^2|B'|^2\) is a rational function of \(z=e^{i\theta}\) that takes the same value at the points of every fibre of \(B\) on the circle. Each component of the curve \(\{B(z)=B(w)\}\) contains infinitely many such pairs, so the equality holds everywhere, and a rational function that is constant on all the fibres of \(B\) is a rational function of \(B\).

  2. Counting poles. The square of the speed may only have poles at the centre (and at infinity). At the other zeros of \(B\), the pole of \(\Phi\circ B\) must be compensated, which forces \(K\cdot M\le2\), where \(K\) is the degree of \(\Phi\). At each critical point outside the zeros, \(\Phi\) must vanish, which uses up its \(K\) zeros inside the disk: \(W\le K\). What remains at the centre is a pole of order \(m\cdot K\), the number of harmonics.

  3. Construction. The product above has degree \(K=W\) and satisfies every condition.

A new proof of Theorem Z. The criterion says that at most two harmonics are needed exactly when \(B\) has one critical value, or two with simple critical points. Since a force with at most two harmonics draws polygons around a conic, and conversely (Jacobi, Griffiths–Harris), this is Theorem Z again, reached through mechanics.

Moving the centre. Composing \(B\) on the right with a disk automorphism moves the centre; the polygons change by a projective map that keeps the circle, and the monodromy does not change. The level of \(B\) is the smallest number of harmonics over all positions of the centre. In degree 4 it separates the four cases exactly:

Degree 4best place for the centrelevel
cyclic \(C_4\)the critical point0
dihedral \(D_4\)a simple point of the fibre with one critical point1
\(S_4\), two critical valuesthe critical point where three sheets meet3
\(S_4\), three critical valuesany critical point4

Level 1 means a pendulum: after moving the centre, every \(D_4\) product draws polygons around a circle. A generic product of degree 5 or more has infinite level, wherever the centre is.

3. A level for every product: the paper picture

To give every Blaschke product a finite level, count defects instead of harmonics. The square of the time element, \(dt^2\), is always the pull-back by \(B\) of an object \(Q\) of the same kind on the target disk. Measured with this time, the disk becomes a surface of flat paper, except at a few points:

  • at a simple pole of \(dt^2\) the paper is folded: the total angle is half a turn (a corner);
  • at a zero of order \(k\) the total angle is \(k+2\) half-turns: there is extra paper.

The rational level proof outlined

Theorem. The smallest amount of extra paper, over all motions that draw the polygons of a Blaschke product of degree \(n\), is \[ \min\bigl(\,2(n-1-R)\ ,\ \ell_1+\ell_2-2\,\bigr), \] where \(R\) is the largest total ramification above a single value, and \(\ell_1+\ell_2\) the smallest total number of simple points in two fibres.

Why: inside the disk, the orders of \(Q\) always add up to \(-2\), by symmetry with respect to the circle. So \(Q\) has one double pole or two simple poles there; any other choice adds zeros of \(Q\), which cost more than they save. A point of local degree \(e\) above a point where \(Q\) has order \(k\) carries order \(e(k+2)-2\), and adding these up gives the two terms.

Level 0, no extra paper, is exactly Theorem Z. For a product with two critical values, that is, a plane tree, the formula becomes

\[ \text{level}=\min\bigl(\text{leaves}-2\ ,\ 2(c-1)\bigr), \]

where \(c\) is the number of vertices of the smaller colour. The picture behind it is a cylinder of paper. Its bottom edge is the circle; its top edge is cut into \(2n\) equal pieces and sewn to itself, and the seam is the tree. Every edge of the tree has the same length in time, and every vertex lies at the same height above the circle: 6.1985 for the fork below, 5.1902 for a tree with four leaves of degree 6, whichever path is used to measure it.

corner (a leaf, white circle in the figures)extra paperthe circle, bottom of the cylinder

This picture is a known one for Shabat polynomials (Strebel differentials, square-tiled surfaces). Here it explains several results of this page at once: Theorem Z (no extra paper), the canonical annulus (the cylinder, wound \(n\) times onto the target cylinder), and the parameter \(\tau\) of Chiu and Ng (height over circumference).

4. The integer sequences

Sorting Blaschke products with two critical values by level means sorting plane trees. All trees below have \(n\) edges and are counted up to rotation: two trees that are mirror images of each other count twice unless stated otherwise.

Known sequences.

  • \(P(n)\), plane trees with \(n\) edges: \(P(n)=\) A002995\((n+1)\): 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 14, 34, 95, 280, 854, 2694, ...
  • The same up to rotation and reflection: A006082\((n+1)\) (called “projective plane trees” there): 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 27, 65, 175, 490, 1473, ...
  • \(R(n,k)\), plane trees rooted at a corner with \(n\) edges and \(k\) leaves: \(R(n,k)=\dfrac{2}{n-1}\dbinom{n-1}{k-2}\dbinom{n}{k}\), which is entry \((n,k-2)\) of A108838 (formula also in this paper on cyclic sieving).
  • Trees with exactly 3 leaves: \(T(n,3)=\) A007997\((n+2)\) \(=\lceil (n-1)(n-2)/6\rceil\); up to reflection as well, A001399\((n-3)\), partitions of \(n-3\) into at most 3 parts.

The triangle \(T(n,k)\): trees by number of leaves

Definition. \(T(n,k)\) is the number of plane trees with \(n\) edges and \(k\) leaves, up to rotation. Formula (Burnside's lemma applied to the rooted trees \(R(n,k)\)):

\[ T(n,k)=\frac1{2n}\Bigl[R(n,k)+\sum_{\substack{d\ge2\\ d\mid n,\ d\mid k}}\varphi(d)\,2\binom{n/d}{k/d}\binom{n/d-1}{k/d-1} +\epsilon\, n\,N\bigl(\tfrac{n-1}{2},\tfrac k2\bigr)\Bigr], \]

where \(\varphi\) is Euler's function, \(N(h,\ell)=\frac1h\binom h\ell\binom h{\ell-1}\) a Narayana number, and \(\epsilon=1\) when \(n\) is odd and \(k\) even, \(0\) otherwise. The middle sum counts the trees with a rotation of order \(d\) around a vertex (the folding of the figure above); the last term counts the trees with a half-turn around the middle of an edge.

The triangle \(L(n,j)\): trees by level

Definition. \(L(n,j)\) is the number of plane trees with \(n\) edges, up to rotation, whose level \(\min(\text{leaves}-2,\ 2(c-1))\) equals \(j\). Equivalently, the number of combinatorial types of Blaschke products of degree \(n\) with two critical values that need extra paper \(j\) (each type is a one-parameter family, the parameter being the distance between the two critical values).

  • \(L(n,0)=2\): the chain and the star, the two cases of Theorem Z.
  • \(L(n,1)=T(n,3)=\) A007997\((n+2)\) for \(n\ge4\): level 1 means exactly three leaves.
  • The highest level is \(n-3\). It is reached only by “double stars” (two adjacent centres carrying all the leaves, split as evenly as possible): 1 tree when \(n\) is even, 2 when \(n\) is odd.
In the OEIS? I searched the whole OEIS database (the official data on GitHub, 401,397 sequences, November 2026) for every row and column above, read in both directions. The totals, the rooted triangle and the 3-leaf column are there, as listed. The triangle \(T(n,k)\), its columns for 4, 5 and 6 leaves, all the columns of \(L(n,j)\), and their versions up to reflection are not.
Status. The proposition of part 1 is proved. The harmonic criterion and the rational level are proved in outline above; full write-ups are still to come. The formula for \(T(n,k)\) is proved: the folding argument reduces the symmetric trees to rooted trees with a marked vertex, and the remaining binomial identity was checked symbolically. The degree-4 table, the heights on the cylinder and the level table were computed numerically or by exhaustive listing. In the literature, the porism for an arbitrary circle map conjugate to a rotation is close to Hungerbühler and Wasem; the identity \(|B'|=\sum P_{a_j}\) is classical; I found no trace of the Blaschke clock as a force, of the harmonic criterion or of the level.

Read the paper

The full article gives the proofs of Theorems X, Y and Z, and the construction of the examples. Theorem Z and its monodromy form, Theorem Z′, are my own results; the paper is written so that the proof of Theorem Z (Section 5) can be read on its own, with a self-contained introduction to the tools for readers who have never met Riemann surfaces or elliptic curves.
